To carry this burden. Furthermore, it is not something that can be briefly grasped or comprehended; nothing can strip it away. Nevertheless, we cannot avoid the fact that our own school has been swept away to its very foundations.
Holding up his staff, he said: "Setting aside the ancients for a moment, how should one act today? He then leaned the staff against the wall and said:
"What is seen nearby is not as good as what is heard from afar."
That evening’s informal discourse: Dawn I clothe myself in the clouds of Beishan; at dusk I lodge in the rain of Beishan.
Having come to be a person of Beishan, you must discern the Master of Beishan. Holding up his whisk, he said:

"If you have already passed the barrier of Yuanwu, ascended the hall of Baoshan, and entered the chamber of the direct transmission, you will naturally gaze face-to-face with the host of these mountains. Amidst the harmonious air of the spring breeze, I venture to ask:"
Before the Great Being Bao Gong had even opened his mouth, how could he have been described? He could not be depicted; he could not be painted.
Do you wish to know where he lands? "The wind blows and the grass bends—who can entrust this to another? The water drops and the ice forms—only one knows it oneself. Again, he cites:
The Great Being Bao Gong said, "The Great Way is right before one's eyes, yet for all its presence, it is difficult to see."
[Dongshan] said, "If you wish to recognize the true essence of the Great Way, it is not apart from sound, form, and speech. He then held up a finger and said, "This is form.
He struck the meditation seat and said, "This is sound. As for speech, it is what is being spoken. But where is the true essence of the Great Way?
You must urgently look with your own eyes at the immortal; do not look at the fan in the immortal’s hand."
Ascending the hall: "Drops drip from the eaves, clear and distinct. What a fine piece of the Patriarch’s mind—unprovoked, it has already fallen into disarray.
Take, for instance, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara: he buys a sesame cake with money; when he lets go of his hand, it turns out to be a piece of raw iron.
Wherein lies the mystery?"
Upon receiving a letter from the Venerable Chijue of Xuefeng, he ascended the hall and said: "A guest has come from the capital city, holding a letter from Fujian that says:
'The cliffs of Shimen are treacherous and its iron gates are secure; how can they compare to the ten-thousand-fathom height of the Coiled Dragon?
The hornless iron ox cannot block it, yet it climbs the Elephant Bone Peak to stir up the waves. "Great assembly, Xuefeng’s ball is rolling—step back!"
"Who is it that cuts the nameplate?
He ascends the hall. "Is it so? Is it not so? It is neither so nor not so. They pass each other with shoulders touching; they return hand-in-hand. Nanquan does not step out from his quarters.
Why eat oil-cakes at Zhuang? Now and then are one and the same time. Those who know the sound will know it; after that, who else shall know?

[He] ascended the hall and raised the following case: A monk asked Touzi, "Regarding the equal cultivation of concentration and wisdom to clearly see the Buddha-nature—what is the principle of this? Touzi...

Huangbo replied: "Throughout the twelve periods of the day, you must not rely upon or depend on a single thing; only then will you attain it."
The Master said: "The questions are identical, yet the answers differ. Those who study Huangbo must see Touzi;
those who see Touzi must study Huangbo. Even if one were to pass through both with a single thread, the staff of Jiangshan would still not nod its head."
Ascending the hall, he said: "How far away is the Way? It is true in every encounter. How distant are the sages? They are divine the moment one embodies them.
When Baizhang was struck by a shout, his ears were deaf for three days; when Shuilao was trampled, he rose up and laughed aloud. How does this compare to 'finger-pointing Zen'?"
"One lifetime’s enjoyment will never be exhausted. [The Master] gave a shout and said, "Juzhi has arrived!

in the Sahā world, sound serves as the site of enlightenment. This assembly of mine, without leaving its original place, traverses forty-two Ganges-sands of worlds."

Traveling through lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, he personally reached the World Above, where he satiated himself with various fragrances. In the space of a single moment, more than two thousand one hundred years had passed.
Upon returning to his original location, he listened to the exposition of the wondrous Dharma. Suddenly, the talkative old Vimalakīrti addressed him, saying:
"That which you bestow is not called a field of merit; those who make offerings to you will fall into the three evil realms. Furthermore, what do you say to this? Only—
Turn toward the Way! Be ashamed, be ashamed! Ascending the hall:
The Dragon coils at Zhongfu; the Tiger crouches at Shicheng. Mount Niushou stretches out before us; Fangshan dwells by our side.
Upon the Zhengzhuan Pavilion, I gazed once and, without realizing it, my brows knit together. Why is this? The waters of the Qianhuai River flow westward in a single stream.
Ascending the hall, the Master raised the case of Master Qingyuan. A monk asked, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma?
Qingyuan replied, "What is the price of rice in Luling? The Master offered this verse: The price of rice in Luling has no high or low; To accept it directly is already late.
How many brokers and peddlers Come to calculate the difference by a hair’s breadth in a pint or a quart!
Ascending the hall, he took up his staff, struck it once, and said: "Before the seven Buddhas, it was just like this. He struck it again and said:
"After the seven Buddhas, it is likewise so. He struck it once more: "A single cloud rises in the late valley; a solitary crane descends from the vast heavens."
Ascending the hall, he said: "If the Sovereign of Mind remains unmoving, the six realms are naturally at peace.

Ascending the hall, he said: "Matters do not have a single direction; wisdom has a thousand variations. Sometimes one strikes at one and stands firm at two;

Dongshan said, "Why not go to a place where there is no cold or heat to avoid them? The monk asked, "What is the place where there is no cold or heat? Dongshan said, "When it is cold, it is cold."

"Kill the *ācārya*! Kill the *ācārya* when it is hot! When it is hot, kill the *ācārya*! The Master said, "Under the gate of Dongshan, the five ranks of the orthodox and the oblique intermingle and penetrate one another.
Although the orthodox position is orthodox, it is nonetheless oblique; although the oblique position is oblique, it is nonetheless orthodox.
Ultimately, what is the place where there is neither cold nor heat? He gave a shout and said, "Do not nod off!"
Ascending the hall, he said: "This is the pivot of the present moment, not a dharma of the immediate eye. At times I let go in two directions and cast out in three;
at other times I chop through nails and cut off iron. As for the ancient saying: 'When one ascends to the height of nine fathoms, I am there with them;
when one is trapped in the depths of the nine abysses, I am there with them. What matter on the periphery does this clarify? After a long silence, he said: 'Not only is it desolate...'"
From within the grass, he entered yet another deep village.
At the rear hall, he ascended the seat before the assembly. He raised the following case: Under Zhaozhou, two monks pushed each other, neither being willing to serve as the First Seat.
The Hall Master informed Zhaozhou of this, and Zhaozhou said, "I will have them both serve as the Second Seat. The Hall Master asked, "Then who shall serve as [the First Seat]?"

The First Seat. Zhaozhou said, "Incense, prepare some. After the head of the monastery had prepared the incense, Zhaozhou said, "The fragrance of precepts, the fragrance of concentration, and the fragrance of wisdom.
The Master [Dongshan] said, "The old man Zhaozhou usually says that elsewhere it is difficult to see but easy to recognize, whereas here it is easy to see but difficult to recognize.
To examine this closely, it is like selling flour mixed with bran. At that time, he was waiting for him to say, "Prepare the incense."
[The Master] said: "I simply say to him: 'This is precisely the second seat. Is there anyone who still feels dissatisfied?
Qingmiao ascended the hall and cited Master Dongshan, who said: "A plot of vacant land before the mountain; With palms joined, I earnestly ask my forefather:
How many times have you sold it only to buy it back? Out of pity for the pines and bamboo, it draws in the pure breeze. —Lingyuan.

The Master said: "The Abbot added a commentary, saying: 'Having mastered the land before the mountain, one finds peace and ease; this is the patriarchal estate. Heaven and earth have no outer boundaries;
pines and bamboos possess the pure breeze. The Master said: 'These two great elders knew only the joy of the pure breeze among pines and bamboos.'"
Yet they do not know the hardships of plowing and reaping. This mountain monk shall now mimic their efforts: each person has a sitting mat of land;
though they occupy it, it was inherited from their ancestors. Measuring its four boundaries, one can never exhaust them; till the fields in due time and await the autumn wind.
Ascending the hall, he said: "The gateway is steep and precipitous; the road is plain and white. There is Muzhou with his shoulder-board and Luzu facing the wall.
Whether you come from the south or the north, whether you go east or west, you must believe that for a long time he has not stepped outside his door."
Ascending the hall, he said: "As soon as there is right and wrong, one becomes distracted and loses one's mind. All of you, when you open your eyes, your thoughts fly about in confusion;
when you close your eyes, your dreams and spirits are restless. But how can you avoid this? After a long silence, he said: 'Pointless, pointless!'"
Ascending the hall, he said: "Sitting atop the heads of the thousand sages, yet at the very bottom of the three miserable realms;
not entangled by myriad conditions, nor guarding one's own self—even if you act thus or otherwise, it is still merely the 'bottom line' spoken of by Xuansha."
Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised the following case: Attendant Wang visited Linji, and they went together before the Sangha Hall.
The Attendant asked, "Do these monks in this hall study the scriptures? Linji said, "They do not study the scriptures. The Attendant asked, "Then do they practice seated meditation?
Linji said, "They do not practice seated meditation. The Attendant asked, "Ultimately, what do you have them do? Linji said, "I have them all become Buddhas and Patriarchs."
The Attendant said, "Though gold dust is precious, when it falls into the eye, it becomes a cataract. Linji said, "I took you for a common man.
The Master said, "There is a gentleman within the gate; now a gentleman arrives at the gate.

While it is not that the Attendant, manifesting in the body of a high official, lacked the ability to stimulate and clarify this matter with Linji, if one examines it closely, he still lacks one move. Tell me, where does this lie in the Attendant’s own division?
Above. From the lineage of Linji. Let those with eyes try to examine this.

Entering the hall: "Makhadeva shut his room; clearly he was wearing horns and holding up his head. Vimalakīrti declined to speak; how could this be merely rolling down the flag and withdrawing the battle array?
A clear faculty upon the palm; a bright mirror on its stand. What about that one phrase? 'Barefoot, treading through frost and snow.'"
Only then does one know the bone-chilling cold.
Entering the hall, [the Master said: "Sewing the collar from the sleeve, or cutting the lapel from under the arm—all these are merely ordinary tailoring.

But as for setting aside the scissors and the ruler, where else would you go to search? After a long silence, he said: "Clouds rise over the Southern Mountain; clouds rise over the Northern Mountain."
Ascending the hall for instruction: Last night at Cold Spring Pavilion, the various pavilions from before and after came to pay their respects.

In this mountain hall, with the breeze gentle and the sun warm, we crossed the eastern and western ravines, ascended the northern and southern peaks, observed the tides at the Sea Gate, and cupped the moon of West Lake in our hands.
Suddenly hearing the third watch and the third *danda*, they unconsciously dispersed in a state of confusion. Why is this so? Because they turn back and further entangle one another;
otherwise, they would abide according to their respective positions.
Ascending the hall, the Master raised the example of Dongshan Yanzu. One day, as he ascended the hall, he made a hand gesture and said, "A jumble, a jumble!
What is it? He then said himself, "The thunder rolls. The Master remarked, "Dongshan speaking thus was like applying the ordinances of summer to spring."
The Buddha ascended the hall for his final teaching on the occasion of his *nirvāṇa*. "Those who see me by means of form, or seek me by means of sound, these people follow a deviant path.
At the very end, he rubbed his chest with his hand and addressed the assembly, saying: "Observe well my purple-golden body. Today it exists; tomorrow it will be no more.
This old fellow has revealed his shadow in two places and stretched out his body in one. Now tell me—"
"This is the one before you; this is the one behind you. Ascending the hall, he said:
"The spring mountains are green, the spring waters are lush. Standing alone on a precarious pavilion, one can never look enough. The apricot blossoms are white, the peach blossoms are red;
though they share the same hue, they are yet not the same. Only Han Shan knows this; clapping his hands, he sings and laughs as he approaches."
Spring Breeze.

Ascending the hall on the fifteenth day of the intercalary second month: The words of Vulture Peak are now entrusted; the mind penetrates the ten directions, spanning the present and piercing through antiquity.
For those who have not yet returned from their journey, morning follows evening again and again. If one does not become intoxicated in the Peach Blossom Village, one will surely enter [the Way].
At the Apricot Blossom Valley, how is it that they call out to one another again and again? "Let us go drink tea beneath Flying Eagle Peak.

Ascending the hall, the Master raised the case of Elder Daoyu, who said: "When everyone gathers together to eat a spoonful of porridge, if you call it 'a spoonful of porridge,' you will enter hell as fast as a shot arrow.
The Master said: "Since it is indeed eating a spoonful of porridge, why does he not call it 'one spoonful'?"
"Pickled vegetables! Here you go, gnawing here and there. If you suddenly bite into it, you will enter hell as fast as a shot arrow. Ascending the hall, he said: "O Great Assembly!
This majestic appearance—straight nose, slanted eyes—what do you call this? Do you call it the 'Formless Diamond Mahāsattva'? Hungry, one eats; thirsty, one drinks;
weary, one lies down; vigorous, one walks. Furthermore, what do you call this? Do you call it the 'True Person of No Station'?"
Someone from among the assembly stepped forward and said, "Venerable sir, do not act so foolishly. [The Master] replied, "I simply say that tomorrow there will be no communal labor (pǔqǐng).

He then ascended the hall and said, "One who does not crave the taste of fragrant bait may truly be called a dragon in a clear pool. Raising his whisk, he said, "Is there anyone here who will leap over the waves?"
"Surging waves! Do you present your head and horns?
He ascended the hall and said: "Citing the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū: 'For ten kalpas he sat at the site of enlightenment, yet the Buddha-dharma did not manifest before him;
he could not attain the Way of Buddhahood. The Master’s verse says: 'Countless people practice to become Buddhas, yet when they press their eyes, everything is nothing but floating flowers.'"
Having sat for ten kalpas, one still remains bashful; I did not expect that by striking the grass, I would startle the snake.
Entering the hall: "In this way, in this way—the nose straight and the eyes askance. Not in this way, not in this way—three heads and eight arms."
Thus it may be; not thus it may also be. A dull bird perches in the reeds; a weary fish rests in the shallows.
Thus it may not be; not thus it may also not be. If one were to shed tears again and again, even the vast ocean would surely dry up.
Ascending the hall, he held up his staff and showed it to the assembly, saying: "At Vulture Peak, a single net was spread that covers the heavens.
Whether you can speak or cannot speak, everyone is right here within it. But as for those who cannot be caged and cannot be summoned back—how do you deal with them?
He struck the ground once with the staff and said: "Caught in one fell swoop."
Ascending the hall, he said: "The heavy gates have not yet been opened; they are a hundredfold and a thousandfold. When the ten thousand doors are all open, there are seven holes and eight apertures.

But what of it when the ten thousand doors have not yet opened? After a long silence, he said: "I thought that mountains and rivers stood as barriers, but coming and going occurs within a single speck of dust."
Because of the snow, he ascended the hall. Six years on the green mountains, at Shaolin in the dead of night—he dwelt within clarity, yet not within clarity.
He pointed to the limit of the single color, yet did not linger at the limit of the single color. Filling the valleys and filling the ditches, it pervades heaven and covers the earth.
But as for these flakes that do not fall elsewhere—when Master Pang clapped his hands, what then? "At nightfall, each knows the cold for himself."
It is cold. Do not wait until the snow reaches three feet deep, waist-high.
Entering the hall, he raised the following case: When Guishan was standing in attendance upon Baizhang, it was late at night. Baizhang said, "Look into the brazier—is there fire or not?"
Guishan said, "There is none. Baizhang went off by himself and, digging deeply, found a small spark of fire. Holding it up, he said, "You said there was none; here it is!
The next day, while they were walking in the mountains, Baizhang asked, "Have you brought the fire? Guishan replied, "I have brought it."
He then picked up a branch of firewood, blew on it twice, and passed it to Baizhang. Baizhang said, "It is like an insect gnawing through wood.
The Master said, "Since leaving Mount Ling, the old man of Mt. Mui has been a king three times; he has lost the head of the discourse."
Yet, here one has mistakenly fixed upon the zero-point of the scale; thus, it becomes all the more devoid of connection.

Today, as the furnace is opened, whether the seeds of fire exist or not, we cannot help but examine them ourselves. He then raised his whisk and blew upon it, saying: "The moment for a spontaneous composition has arrived;
this is by no means merely copying a gourd from a model."
After the formal thanks, the Hall Master and the Ritual Director ascend the hall. The second seat is assigned within the Tuṣita Palace; the public case remains present.
A single bowl of rice is taken from the world of Fragrant Accumulation; the pure regulations remain intact, clearly visible to all eyes.
If one asks for proof: after a long silence, he says: "The moonlight is seen in stillness; the sound of the spring is heard in seclusion."
Ascending the hall, he said: "One is not one; two is not two. Looking up, one does not see the sky; looking down, one does not see the earth.
Speaking thus, there is some clarity amidst the turbidity. "One is indeed one; two is indeed two. Looking up, one sees the blue sky."
"Lowering one's head, one also sees the ground. To speak in such a manner is to have some turbidity within what is already clear. Tell me, assembly, what do you say?
"It is muddy and turbid; it is clear and distinct. After a long silence, he said: "Gathered back into the preceding category.
On the twenty-first day of the sixth month in the tenth year of Chunyou, while at the temple, he accepted the invitation from Mount Jing and offered thanks for receiving the Imperial Edict.
The grace ceremony concluded. He ascended the hall and said: "An aged sandalwood tree within a sandalwood forest has seen many winds and frosts and does not count the passing springs.
Thinking itself worn out and of no further use, it is once again refreshed by the rain and dew."
Taking leave of the assembly, I ascended the hall. Having come to this mountain by the convergence of conditions, seven years have passed since then.

I have been sustained by the support of all you venerable seniors, through which we have roughly established a monastic community. The gathering of our robes and alms bowls has indeed doubled compared to before; may these illusory karmic conditions continue to flourish in the future.
Cloud-palaces rise steeply; moon-temples soar aloft. Two stupas have been newly renovated, and five pavilions restored to their former state.

The missing scriptures have been made complete once more, and the damaged icons have been freshly refurbished. All of these things have their own origins; how could the mountain’s heart forget its sense of gratitude?
I am ashamed that in my old age I do not know when to stop, yet there is this journey to Shuangjing which allows for no evasion;

it is by the command of the Son of Heaven. Now, as the heat of the summer reaches its peak and the special envoy urges me to depart, I cannot help but part for a short while from the venerable assembly of this mountain and the practitioners of Chan from all quarters.
May each of you maintain your practice; fundamentally, there is no difference between separation and union.
How could there be any signs of coming or going? It is further said: "Cloud-palaces and moon-temples upon lapis lazuli ground; a single mind that dwells nowhere and relies on nothing.
Do not say we meet and then part again; when we see each other once more in years to come, it will be exactly as it is now."
Record of the Discourses at Xingsheng Wanshou Chan Temple in Jingshan, Lin’an Prefecture.

"How would you respond to this? the Master asked. The monk said, "Do you not wish to pull the tiger’s whiskers? The monk bowed. The Master said, "I grant you thirty blows.
The Master then raised his whisk and addressed the assembly, saying, "This Dharma-seal of mine is spoken for the sake of benefiting the world.
For fifty years I have traveled as a pilgrim, and for thirty years I have served as abbot; yet I have never once moved it."
Today, having arrived at the summit of Lingxiao and the Chan grove of Shuangjing, we are returning hand-in-hand with all of you on this very day.

Striking the meditation seat with his whisk, he said: "If you all see thus, know thus, believe and understand thus, and uphold thus, then the mountain monk’s entry into the monastery—this entire Buddhist service—will not have been in vain; it is truly worthy."
To repay both requited and unrequited kindnesses, one assists in the transformation of non-action (*wuwei*). Again, [the Master] strikes the whisk and says:
"Let us set this matter aside for now. He then raises another point: When Zen Master Fozhao resided at this mountain, Emperor Xiaozong issued an imperial decree asking:

"When the World-Honored One entered the mountains to cultivate the Way, he accomplished his practice in six years. What was it that he accomplished? Fozhao replied: "I shall explain it for Your Majesty."
[The monk] forgot [the question]. The Master said: "Xiaozong emptied his belly and poured out his guts to fortify the Buddhist Way;
Fozhao, with head tucked in and feet tucked up, faced the situation directly when the opportunity arose. This was certainly not for nothing, but what exactly was accomplished?
'From of old, no one has recognized the merit of his labor; he simply wishes to reassert his epoch-making achievements.'"
Ascending the hall, he called to the assembly, saying: "Since I came from Lingyin to ascend this mountain, I have had the opportunity to meet with you all.
I possess nothing at all; I carry only a single bottle of water from the East Ravine and a few fragments of clouds from the Southern and Northern Mountains."
Today, I bring this forth as an offering of equality. Someone might say: "Where are there no such things among the green mountains?
Why must you go to such lengths to accommodate people's sentiments? To this, I simply reply: "Do not take offense at my meagerness. [I shall now] stand for a long while.
Ascending the hall, he said: "I have a phrase. Everywhere and in every place, lift it up and it is divided; let it go and it is gathered.
With both hands I bring it forth, and with one hand I deliver it. Jiangxi once had a saying. He struck the meditation seat and said: "Take this as the master."
Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised the case of Mazu. One day, Mazu ordered Zhizang to deliver a letter to Jingshan. When Jingshan received the letter and opened it, he saw a single circle;
he then placed a dot in the center and sealed it back. When National Teacher Huizhong heard of this, he said, "Master Qin was still deluded by Master Ma.
Later, Xuedou said, "Xuedou’s insight is something I want everyone to know together. It is simply..."
This horse-master was already deluded when he first drew [the bow]. The Master said: "In the peaceful world of Jiangxi, they rashly stir up war;
at Jingshan, having long experienced military formations, no extra effort is required; Nanyang could not restrain his impatience and joined in for his share;
Xuedou, a master who has upheld the lineage for a generation, yet upon reaching this point, acts like a novice on his first journey."
[The Master] spoke: "This too caused the price of paper to soar in Hangzhou.
When the two classes of attendants took their places upon the high seat, they saw that the Great Being Avalokiteśvara possesses eighty-four thousand *mudrā* arms."
"It is indeed beautiful; yet it is like making a single-sided vest—where would one put all these sleeves?

How much better it is for Jing Mountain to have its own various affairs, where everyone extends a hand so that naturally nothing remains undone. Though it is said, 'The wealthy find even a thousand mouths too few.'"
Master Xie received the invitation to ascend the hall on the first day of the eighth month. What a fine report this is! After long rains, the first clearing is announced;

a fresh coolness arises throughout the eight directions. The rice and grain fill the fields, urging people to harvest early. Grain by grain, seed by seed—treasure them well; do not let them lie scattered and wasted across the earth.
Wait until last year’s and this year’s rents, both public and private, [are all settled].
When the meal is finished, one may forget a hundred hungers in a single satiation. With drumming bellies and songs of praise, one passes the remaining day.
But tell me, how does one sing? "Joy! Joy!"
Returning to the Hall from the Mountain Village: For a month we have been parted, yet I have not left the gate. How many times have we passed through flowering counties and smoky villages?

Within the shadows of mulberry and hemp, the fragrance of cooking rice rises early; Amidst the shade of pines and bamboo, laughter and conversation are warm. The secluded chime leaves at dawn as I welcome the white sun.
Sparse bells ring out as we moor for the evening, sending off the twilight. The banners are furled and the ranks withdrawn; it is time to return. Who is it that recognizes kindness and repays it?
Ascending the hall: On the fifteenth day of the tenth month, withered leaves pile up like clouds, and the cold wind pushes against the door. Beneath the bright window is the toilet.
Head. Whether walking east or walking west, this is the very place of upholding [the Dharma]. Those who investigate the mystery must take this to heart. As the ancients said:

As for the wild brandishing and chaotic shouts, the blind staff and the senseless shackles—when examined closely, these are much like scratching an itch through a boot. One error leads to a hundred errors.
Mistakes have been made until now. One family does not mind the affairs of another; a new official does not concern himself with old matters.
Furthermore, beneath my Qingliang Gate, the clouds are deep and the fires are cold; water drips and ice forms. From the beginning, there has been no oil for the paper wick;
the scale-weights are made of pure cast iron. There is nowhere to lift them up; it is utterly impenetrable. Simply let it go like this: limping and dragging along.
A hundred uglinesses, a thousand clumsinesses—gathered in. Clutching and grasping, as if dull-witted or deaf. Mountain upon mountain, water upon water;
misty smoke, drizzling rain. From south to north, from west to east. "The wind follows the tiger, the clouds follow the dragon.
Who cares whether it is three feet deep or three feet wide? This year’s winter, last year’s winter. Winter Solstice.
