At Jiaoshan, on the winter solstice, I hold the whisk—the secret seal of the thousand Buddhas, the profound barrier of the patriarchs, the claws and fangs of all quarters, and the very core of the monk’s realization. (He raises the whisk.)
He said, "It is all right here. He gave a shout and said, "First, you must not look at it with the correct eye; second, you must not let it pass.
Six ears do not share a secret; with a single hand, I entrust it all to you.

If you can truly accept this and carry it out, driving it forward and putting it to use, you shall make the white waves overflow the heavens atop Mount Fuyushan, reaching the gates of the ocean realm."
Inside, the bottom rolls up in dust and filth; Yangzi’s soul is startled, and Shiweng’s gallbladder shrinks with fear. With his whisk, he draws a line and says:
"This groundless, thoroughgoing grandmotherly heart—when cast upon the ground, its golden sound is like that of rubble. Even so, tell me: what do you say?
"How is it when the phrase 'The Way of the gentleman grows long' is uttered? After a long silence, he said: "Calamity does not enter the door of a prudent family.
He then cited the case of Muzhou asking Yangshan: "Mid-winter’s bitter cold is an annual occurrence; as the movement of the sun's shadow shifts, what is the matter?"
Yangshan stepped forward, stood with his hands clasped, and remained there. Guishan said, "I knew you would not be able to answer this question.
Xiangyan said, "I am uniquely capable of answering this question. Guishan asked him as before; Xiangyan likewise stepped forward, stood with his hands clasped, and remained there.
Guishan said, "Fortunately, Jizi does not understand. The verse says: A single pole with a line and two golden hooks.

The fish do not violate the clear waves; their intent is naturally distinct. After they have slantedly dragged their raincoats to cover themselves, there remains only the bright moon filling the rivers and lakes.
Holding the whisk at Mount Jiao during the summer retreat.
To one who contemplates the great ocean, water is difficult to describe; to one who roams the gate of the sages, words are difficult to employ.

Having already entered the gateway of the ocean-kingdom, one further ascends the hall of ocean-clouds. There is not a single drop that can aid its depth; there is not a single word that can assist its eloquence.
Thus it is, thus it is—let us simply plan to sail our boat with the current. Not thus, not thus—then we see the rudder being held against the wind.
In suchness, yet not so; the severed reeds push the moon up to Yangzhou. Not so, yet indeed so; casually shifting the pivot, one returns to that very source.
Like a fragrant elephant cutting through the current, like a golden-scaled fish piercing the net—can you deceive him?
There is not even a single point by which you can. If you are somewhat conversant with the currents of the water, you should, before even a single bubble has arisen, board the great vessel.

This is the boat of aspiration. Hoist the firm and dense sails, follow the pure current, and enter the sea of non-action (*asaṃskṛta*). Directly, you shall attain the confluence of the nine rivers and the tributaries of the hundred valleys;

the moon in the water and the sky will be viewed as one, and wind and clouds will reach a single harmony. This is called mounting the Bodhisattva vehicle and cultivating the practice of cessation (*śānti*).
Within these ninety days, your efforts shall not be in vain. If you examine this closely, how is it any different from killing a melon?
The crane perches in the reeds; the weary fish rests in the marsh. This causes the lame monk to find he cannot restrain his impatience;
with a leap, he ascends to the Thirty-three Heavens, striking the nostrils of Śakra. A carp from the Eastern Sea receives a blow upon its back.
The rain pours down like an overturned basin. A-he-he! The sixty-year sexagenary cycle has fallen into total chaos.
De-yun has run off to another peak; Shancai has suddenly taken his first step. Old Hai-yun, a frozen leech, cannot hold himself steady and rolls amidst a thousand waves and ten thousand ripples.
Not seeing his own nostrils with his eyes, he silently thinks to himself: "I have lived in this land for twelve years."
He observed and contemplated that the great ocean had become his realm; alas, how pitiable it was that today, for no reason, he had suddenly lost it all at once.
At that time, there was an elder monk, a fellow practitioner, who knew his inner depths; although it is difficult to support a false dharma, [he remained steadfast].
He could do nothing but come forward, join his palms, and praise him as excellent. Suddenly picking up his staff, he struck it once and said:
"To play in the tide, one must be a man who plays in the tide.
He then cited Dongshan: "Though the dog has no Buddha-nature, it is still ten thousand times better than the cat. Last night...
The Head Monk said: "Though Old Dongshan was cunning, when examined closely, he fundamentally did not understand.
To say that a dog has no Buddha-nature is worth more than ten thousand times a cat. The Master said: "Speaking in such a way is much like adding to what is fat and subtracting from what is thin;
one does not realize that the old man of Dongshan was merely accustomed to taking advantage of the situation."
At Jangshan during the winter festival, I held the whisk;
this Dharma seal of mine is like poisoned lacquer spread across the courtyard, or a hair-cutting blade within its scabbard—those who aim at it perish, and those who hear of it are lost.
Throughout my travels, I have never recklessly disclosed news of it. Now that we have met on this narrow path for a single occasion, how could it possibly be hidden away in a bag?
He covered [the bowl] for a long while, then said, "Aha! Before the tongue has even moved, it has already been spoken by Dulonggang.
It has been spoken by Yuanwu’s Barrier. It has been spoken by Baoshantang. Setting aside Yuanwu’s Barrier and Baoshantang for a moment—after all, what did Dulonggang say?
Is there anyone here who can hear and perceive it clearly? He then held up his whisk.
[He] finally attained it. Raising his whisk, he said: "A guest comes from the western region, holding a letter from the eastern land.

He reports that mid-winter is bitterly cold, yet the sun reaches its longest path at the winter solstice. Old Hao of Yüquan wears a single piece of cloth trousers that remain as bright red as ever until this very day.
When the frosty sky and moon are cold, the night grows even colder; the spring breeze of the river lands cannot stir it. A-ha!"
Ha! What a fine, holeless iron hammer! To go on just like this—though there are countless [such people] on level ground, how can they pass through the thicket of thorns?
Those who are sharp-witted and skilled at discerning the initial signs need not even slightly kick over the seat itself;
from where in the east, west, south, or north could it have come? Both Buddhas and sentient beings must all beg for their lives. Yet, as for the patch-robed monk...
To the assembly: How far, how very far we have come! As the whisk-wielding abbot, when you raise such a proclamation, is there anyone here who cannot bear it?
He lets out a shout and says: "In the end, this would only serve to prolong the imprisonment and increase one's delusions."
Shushan raised the question for Yunmen, saying, "Bring forth the phrase by which you have attained power. Yunmen said, "Why not ask in a loud voice? Shushan then asked in a loud voice.
Yunmen said, "Did you eat porridge this morning? Shushan said, "How could I not have eaten porridge?
Yunmen said, "Why are you shouting so wildly? At night, the Head of the Hall remarked, "Great indeed is Yunmen, acting right before Shushan's eyes."
He has lost one eye. The Abbot who holds the whisk, tonight at the side of the hawk’s talons, snatches the rabbit away.
Great and small Shushan, in the presence of Yunmen, lost one eye.

At Mount Jangshan, during the summer retreat, when the whisk was held, a single path before the voice could not be glimpsed by a thousand sages; a single thought at the gate of the face could not be covered by a thousand hands. Two thousand years ago...
The awakened ones of old looked up at it, unable to reach it; they vaguely delineated a circle in that indistinct realm and called it the "Monastery of Perfect Enlightenment.
This is much like opening one's eyes and yet dreaming; therein they cause people to mount the Bodhisattva vehicle and cultivate the practice of quiescent extinction.
Do not suppress the noble to become base. For two thousand years, everyone has merely been following along with the coarse woolen cloth.

In the Western Heaven, they observe the *cāturmāsya*; in the Eastern Land, they protect living beings; in the Southern Continent, they practice walking meditation; in the Northern Continent, they sit in silent contemplation.
They claim there is no place left unattended, yet they do not realize that this is precisely like gold dust obscuring the eyes. Can you still escape his circle? After two thousand years...
It is displayed upon the hall of Zhongshan. To take a mistake as a right, one follows the pattern as it comes.

For now, let us have Hanshanzi and the water-buffalo follow the herd for ninety days; drinking when thirsty and eating when hungry, guarding the beginning and protecting the end, let us pass the time in this manner.
Do not allow yourself to become dazed or drowsy, lest at the moment of a doze you be bitten by the sound of the bell and turned over once more by the seven-strip robe.
He knocks down the monks’ hall and shatters the Buddha hall until all people throughout the great earth have their eyes askance and noses straight.
While it is not that he cannot carry them away in a single cloth bag, suddenly the Great Being Jingrong tears off his mask and laughs heartily, saying:
"What a fuss and commotion! It remains, as ever, within his own circle. With a shout, he lets out a roar.
[The Master] said: "What is this 'talking in one's sleep'?
He then cited Nanquan’s question to Huangbo: "Regarding the study of the equality of concentration and wisdom and the clear seeing of Buddha-nature—how is this principle? Huangbo replied:
"Throughout the twelve periods of the day, one must not rely upon or depend on a single thing before it can be attained. Nanquan said, "Is this not your own realization, Elder?
Baizhang replied, "I dare not say so. Nanquan said, "Setting aside the cost of rice gruel for a moment, who will pay for the straw sandals?"
Huangbo said, "Stop. The Master said, "These two great elders possessed lofty merit and renowned fame; they were fit to be discussed in the imperial court.
Why, then, do you speak of them as if they were words from the desks of common students? When it comes to turning the tongue upside down, one sees at once that when the wind blows, the grass bows.
To call Huangbo’s 'stopping' a 'trap for tigers'—you have not even dreamed of it."
At Jangshan, during the summer retreat, he held the whisk;

whether one attains the Way or not, the Holy Truths are vast and empty—yet one still does not recognize them. If Jinling were willing to come again, nine years of facing the wall would have been in vain.
Whether one knows it or does not know it, this single round pearl has been luminous for a long time. He tears open the old skin: one!
Fang still left something lingering. He looked around at the assembly and said, "Do you wish to see the two great elders, Jingrong and Biyan?
For ninety days of a summer retreat, they have drunk when thirsty and eaten when hungry; they have walked when vigorous and slept when weary.

They rested their heads on Tiantai and stepped upon Nanyue; they bowed to Emei and leaned against Wutai. The wind cannot enter them, and the rain cannot touch them. Yet, they never departed from this very place. Why is this so?"
He lifted his foot but did not set it down, then gave a shout and said: "The way is open! Tiantai remains Tiantai;
Nanyue remains Nanyue; Emei remains Emei; Wutai remains Wutai. The oceanic Peng bird spans ninety thousand li; the Liaodong crane lives for three thousand years."
Nor does it emerge from here. For what reason can one not set foot [within it]? He lets out a shout and says:
"If you can penetrate this entirely, whether I let you pass or not is entirely in the hands of Jiangshan. Why? Because the guest listens while the host decides."
[The Master] raised a case where a monk asked Yunfeng, "In the Western Heavens, they use a wax figure as proof; in this land, what is used as proof?
Yunfeng said, "An iron pellet. The Master said, "Yunfeng’s single pellet was enough to cause all the wax figures of the five heavens to melt away completely."
If one is not forged from tempered steel, do not be careless.
At Lingyin, on the winter solstice, I wield the whisk;
at Lingju’s One Peak, my true face is fully revealed. Cold Spring’s dripping water is a ready-made koan. Sometimes it is thus.
The sea is vast and the mountains are remote; the wind is clear and the moon is bright. Yet there are times when it is not so: waves overturn and billows surge; lightning strikes and thunder roars.

A thousand postures and ten thousand manifestations appear or vanish according to the occasion. Thus, much emptiness does not equal a little reality; what is seen nearby far surpasses what is heard from afar.
Master Ma blinked his eyes and raised his eyebrows; Shishuang gnashed his teeth; they struck the meditation seat and held up their fly-whisks—these acts are all in accord with the Way.
Water and mud; here, the dark meets the bright. All of this is merely a temporary crossroads. One must wait until the six yin lines are stripped away and the single yang line arises.
As for the withered tree and cold vine knowing cold and heat by themselves—let that be set aside for now. But as for what the Elder of the Abbot’s Quarter said:
“The staff of Deshan is low; the shout of Linji is faint. What is the meaning of this? After a long silence, he said: “Holding it in hand...”
The Night-Bright Talisman: How many know when day breaks?
A monk asked Shishuang, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? Shishuang gnashed his teeth to indicate it.
Later, the monk asked Jiufeng, "What was the meaning of the former master gnashing his teeth? Jiufeng said, "It would be better to cut out one's tongue than to violate the state."

Huì asked Yúngài again. Yúngài said, "What enmity do I have with my former master? The Master said, "In Shíshuāng’s way of employing people, one's life was as precarious as a thread suspended from above.
Had you not both sons joined your efforts to support him, he would inevitably have suffered a lifelong injustice that could never be cleared."
Small Lecture by Chan Master Shixi Fohai while Residing at Ba’en Chan Temple in Jiankang Prefecture;
compiled by Attendant Zhu Xian and others.
Winter Solstice Small Sermon: If you wish to understand the meaning of Buddha-nature, you should contemplate the conditions of time and season.
For now, what do you call "the meaning of Buddha-nature"? What constitutes "the conditions of time and season"? And how do you contemplate it? Simply grasp it as it is.
As the movement of the sun’s shadow shifts, what has ever been stirred? As yin and yang revolve, there is from the start no interruption.

Therefore, when Guishan asked Yangshan, “The bitter cold of mid-winter is an annual occurrence; as for the shifting of the sun’s shadow, what is it like? Yangshan stepped forward with his hands clasped.
Xiangyan likewise stepped forward with his hands clasped. Thus, from being pulled from the left and supported from the right, to dark meeting dark and light meeting light—briefly put: [it is thus].
The immediate opportunity is revealed before one’s eyes, yet it is not a dharma of the present moment. Responding to the time and the season, it illuminates both past and present.
In bestowing gratitude upon the ancients, the gateway is identical, yet the ways of entering and exiting differ.

Nevertheless, with every faltering step and every weary stride, there is not a single moment of wasted time, nor a single instance of effort that fails to reach its ground. Elder, you are none other than all people. All people...
The person is the elder himself. He has accomplished the Buddha-work within a dream and manifested his own radiance;
it can be said that since the time has arrived, the principle reveals itself spontaneously. If it were otherwise, this mountain monk would have betrayed many people.
Once, during a winter night at Dongshan, while he was eating sweetmeats with the Head Seat Taishi, he asked:
"There is a thing that reaches up to heaven and down to earth, black as lacquer; it is ever present within activity, yet it cannot be grasped within activity.
Where do you say its fault lies? The Head Seat replied, "The fault lies within activity. Dongshan said, "Attendant, clear away the table of sweetmeats."
The Master said: "The Old Man of Xinfeng is upright from head to tail; even a thousand years later, his majestic presence remains chilling.

It is not that he lacks gratitude, but simply that he has no attendant to clear away the fruit table. If you have not yet discerned the beginning and end of this matter, you must chew it thoroughly and swallow it slowly."
A small *sōsan* on the eve of the New Year. A monk asked, "What is it like when the year is spent and the age is exhausted? The Master said, "The eyes are horizontal and the nose is straight.
The monk pressed further, "Kaixian said, 'As before, it is still cold in the first month of spring. What about that? The Master said, "It has come along with you."
The monk asked, "Can it be called 'a field that is secure and stable'? The Master said, "A clumsy fellow!
The monk asked, "What about 'Old Wang of the Eastern Village burning paper money at night'? The Master said, "The arrow has already passed over Silla. The monk bowed.
The Master then said: "At the end of the old year and the beginning of the new year, the affairs of kalpas as numerous as dust motes are just like this.

The old Wang of East Village burns paper money at night; when Lord Zhang drinks wine, Lord Li gets drunk. To meet the situation face-to-face and act with immediate presence, one must penetrate to the very top and bottom.
If you wish to know how to pass through the coverlet, you must sleep in the same bed. Although the gate of Guangxiao Temple is propped up here and there, it remains silent and desolate."
Liao! To compare this to cutting firewood and continuing the meditation seat—how could it be anything less than a hundred thousand miles apart? A-he-he! Is it so? Is it not so?
If one is not an old enemy, they do not meet head-on. A pure breeze stirs the earth, its arrival never ceasing.
The Master cited a monk’s question to Xuedou: “What is the one phrase transmitted outside the teachings? Xuedou said, “Look, look! The twelfth lunar month has ended.
The monk said, “In that case, the fragrance will flow forth. Xuedou said, “A mute man eating a bitter melon. The Master commented: “To hold fast where there is release;
to hold fast where there is release. The Old Man of Rurong has experienced much; when asked about retribution, he replied: [He remained silent.]
En: "What is the phrase transmitted outside the teachings? I simply said to him: "Tomorrow is the first day of the lunar month.
[He asked: "In that case, the fragrance will flow forth. [I replied: "Planting rice, yet beans grow."

The Small Sermon for the Closing of the Retreat: "Mind itself is Buddha"—this is, without cause, to wear shackles and carry a yoke. "Neither Buddha nor mind"—this is like avoiding drowning only to leap into fire.
Even when you have picked it up, it does not fall within the realm of conceptual thought; yet to see it at once is already to be two-headed or three-headed.
Taking a light step forward, how could this be anything less than being in the kingdom of Silla? Much less is it merely tracing a pattern or writing in vermilion ink. Let it go!
People follow the red lacquer and fill in the black ink; they have made a mistake, yet they remain complacent.

For now, let us follow him into the sandalwood groves and lion dens—whether five hundred or seven hundred [monks], for long or short periods—shaking the thunder of the Dharma and beating the drum of the Dharma, spreading the clouds of compassion and sprinkling the nectar of immortality.
Ha! Upon the ground of purity, one must not leave things in such a state of disorder.
Regarding Yantou’s visit to Deshan: as soon as he stepped across the threshold, he asked, "Is this ordinary or is it sacred? Deshan gave a shout; Yantou then prostrated himself.
Hearing of this, Dongshan said, "If it were not for Master Huo, it would have been very difficult to handle. Yantou said:
"Old man Dongshan did not recognize good from evil and wrongly applied these words and names. At that time, I would have held one hand up and the other down.
The Master said, "I have long admired Zhou Jin-gang; with his single white staff, he lets no one pass—neither Buddhas nor patriarchs."
For what reason is there such a display of shame today? Dongshan seems truly envious. Let that matter rest for now;
where is the point of raising one hand while clutching down with the other? Those who possess the extraordinary eye that transcends the school—try to discern it!
Small Assembly for the End of Retreat: When reflected in the eye, it is like the thousand suns; the myriad phenomena cannot escape their shadows and forms.
Grasp this directly: the eye does not see its own nostrils. Yet, how is it? To let this one point pass is to ensure that everything is thoroughly settled and cleared away.
Do not allow what has been cut away to grow back; hold it fast with all your might. Do not let what has been severed reconnect.
Though such talk may still carry the scent of milk, suddenly—within the eyes and within the ears—there is no way to evade it.

This is precisely that momentary crossroads where one must let go of both hands and feet. Where could it possibly be contained? As Master Yunmen said: "It reaches to the point where mountains, rivers, and the great earth..."
To be without even a hair’s breadth of fault or affliction is still merely a "turning phrase" (*zhuǎnjù*). Not seeing a single form (*yīshè*) is only half the presentation.
You must know that there is yet a time for the full presentation (*quántí*). As for the full presentation, I dare not speak of it.
Is there anyone who does not see a single form? Sentient beings simply have not yet contemplated; how can you disparage yourselves and become disheartened?

Cuiyan raised his eyebrows and showed them to the assembly, saying, "Throughout this summer, I have been conversing with you brothers; look, are my eyebrows still there? Baofu said, "The heart of a thief is always apprehensive.
Changqing said, "They are growing! Yunmen said, "The barrier. The Master said: Cuiyan has seized his own hair-tuft and presented himself at the yamen;
he has confessed his crime while still in possession of the loot. While it is not that he was incapable of responding in song or skillfully modulating the tone, Baofu’s remark is indeed significant.
Changqing’s establishment of his teaching style—this lame-legged master has something to compare! To pass judgment in such a manner, look:
are Baen’s eyebrows still there?
Winter Solstice Small Lecture: Dust mote by dust mote, world-system by world-system—wherever you strike or bump into them, there is nowhere to avoid it.
Why is it that the Universal Eye entered samādhi three times and, though surveying the entire trichiliocosm, did not see Samantabhadra?
Is it because he exists when in use, yet vanishes entirely when sought? Furthermore, there are those who do not recognize good from evil; tell them to...
A single thought arises within the samādhi of stillness, and suddenly one sees Samantabhadra in the void, riding upon a six-tusked fragrant elephant.

Is this not like pressing on the eyes? Is it not, in fact, quite clear? If you lack even a shred of backbone here, you will inevitably end up crying out in protest while clutching your own stolen goods.
I, Baoren, have never washed soil from within the mud; I cause people to take a step forward in a place where there is no support, pushing them onward.
When you cease all deliberation and investigation, you give rise to doubt and must scrutinize it thoroughly. Day after day, you measure your firewood and count your rice;

you are emaciated by hunger and plagued by clamor, passing your time in this manner alone. What place is there for concealment? If money does not show its tracks and silver does not show its whiteness, who can govern them?
Why is this so? Tomorrow is the winter solstice, when the first yang arises.
Mingzhao raised his staff and addressed the assembly, saying, "The wind here is somewhat stiff; let us return to a warm place to deliberate.

A monk followed him, and as soon as they reached the warmth, Mingzhao said, "As soon as you reach a warm place, you fall asleep," and drove them all away at once with his staff. The Master composed a verse on this:
"Vivid within the mind and eyes amidst the dust of form, Radiant within the dust of form and amidst the mind and eyes. To tear it open directly—"
This is dull-witted. How could one possibly follow the footsteps across ten thousand layers of mountains?
When presiding over the retreat, the small-scale *can* (sermons), and preaching the Dharma, if it does not accord with the capacities of the listeners, it is entirely untimely speech.

Before the assembly, if one speaks of the Three Mysteries and Three Essentials, the Two Hosts and Two Guests, the Five Houses and Ten Schools, or the myriad gates and ten thousand doors, it is merely a matter of polishing and grasping them firmly.

The Eye of Heaven and Earth. A single point awakens the heart that encompasses all things from antiquity to the present. All is but leftover soup and rancid rice; constrained by necessity, I shall briefly reveal a mere fragment.
Yet this is neither the sacred traces of the Seven Buddhas nor the life-vein of the successive patriarchs.
Counting on my fingers, I say: one, two, three, eight, nine, ten. Nine out of ten words are not as good as a single silence. Without cause, two ladles and three ladles are finished. If...
The Way lowers its head and does not look back. Thirty years later, being struck by an arrow will still be like shooting at a person;
you can take it for granted that this will provoke laughter. A monk asked Zhaozhou, "What should I do when I have doubts? Zhaozhou said, "Great doubt, small doubt. The monk said:
"Great doubt," said Zhou. "Great doubt is at the northeast corner; small doubt is behind the Sangha Hall. The Master said, "It is very easy to see, but very difficult to recognize.
This is because one has become accustomed to taking advantage of it."
A Small Sermon on the Retreat: A single, whole phrase is raised together by the ancients and the moderns; four corners and six sides, three peaks and five exposures.
At times it is cast before people, utterly transcending the slightest hair’s breadth; at times it is gathered into a single speck of dust, filling the entire universe.
Those who possess the Three Mysteries and the Three Essentials perceive the entire essence as absolute truth; those who divide the five ranks into ruler and minister engage in a circular interplay.
This is indeed so, yet it is truly regrettable. How can it compare to having a narrow throat that cannot swallow for you, or teeth so obstructed that they cannot spit for you?
Alala! Suffering within pleasure. The Three Mountains nod their heads and turn back; the Qin River flows upstream.
[The words] flow away. Do not say that the opportunity was not granted. Suddenly someone asks, "What about the reward for labor at the end of the three summer months?
After a long silence, he says, "Take this clearly to heart."

[The Master] cited the case of Linji asking a monk, "Where have you come from? The monk said, "From Dingzhou. Linji raised his staff; as the monk hesitated, Linji struck him. The monk did not accept this.
Linji said, "If you meet someone with clear eyes later on, go to them. Later, the monk went to attend upon Sansheng and recounted the previous conversation.
As Sansheng raised his staff, the monk hesitated; Sansheng struck him immediately. The Master said, "Had it not been for Sansheng, Linji would not have attained [his realization]."
"A lifetime without a single trace of snow—will this monk finally accept it or not? He lets out a shout.
A small *can* (sermon) on New Year’s Eve: "I have always said, 'Quick! Quick! Look, look—the thirtieth day of the twelfth month is upon us."
Like a rat climbing a cow’s horn, or a monkey entering a cloth bag;
when all skills are exhausted and the forked path is reached, at such a moment, the pillar swallows the void, and the lantern swallows the pillar.
Suddenly, performing a somersault, one leaps from this side to that—yet "early spring is still cold. *Du!* These are inverted words and upside-down talk.
Mo. [The Master] cites the story of Zhaozhou visiting Zhunyu. Zhaozhou walked up the Dharma Hall from east to west.
Zhunyu asked, "What are you doing? Zhaozhou said, "I am testing the water. Zhunyu said, "There isn't even a single drop here; what are you testing?
Zhaozhou then leaned his staff against the wall and departed. The Master’s verse says: Testing the depth and shallowness before the Hall of Good Dharma— The cold waves are level.
Rising from the earth to a height of a thousand fathoms—probing the pole against the wall and departing. This too is the poor child picking up gold.

At the small *sīmā* (concluding retreat) assembly: falling into other realms, every movement must be the total function. Amidst the flash of a stone struck by lightning, one wears horns and holds up the head.
Within the shadow of a sword’s edge, wind arises from the grass; to behold it is to lose one's heart, and to confront it is to risk one's life.
Who can meet this critical moment? Please, look with urgent clarity! Xuefeng addressed the assembly, saying: "On South Mountain there is a tortoise-nose snake. You all—!"
"You must look well. The Master said, "I once told the venerable elders of Min: 'A bright mirror stands upon its stand; when a Hu comes, a Han appears.
Yet it turns out the snake has entered the bamboo tube—the crooked mind remains. Changqing said, "In the hall today, there are many such people."
To lose one's body and forfeit one's life is to follow head-first with the tail trailing behind. Xuansha said, "What use is Nan-shan?
Unable to support it, Yunmen brandished his staff before Xuefeng and made a gesture of fear. Turning over in the grass—what a pity!
This "tortoise-nose" staff has been completely spoiled by the whole family. When they reached the foot of Lusi Peak, he intended to...
He revived. Then he cried out in a loud voice, "Look underfoot! You have wounded yourself.
"In the beginning, there was one who would have gripped it firmly with a pinch on the seven-inch [handle]; let us see what happens when the fire falls!
He threw down his staff and said, "To the east of Shicheng and to the west of Yecheng—everyone must take care! Is there anyone who will scratch an itch on the head of a venomous snake?"
"Zhe-mo. (He lets out a shout.
He cites the two monks under Master Yinzong who contended over the wind and the banner; one said, "The wind moves," and the other said, "The banner moves.
The Patriarch said, "It is not the wind moving; it is not the banner moving. It is the mind of the worthy one that moves. The Master composes a verse: "It is not the wind..."
It is not the banner. With a dignified wave of the hand, he passes through the heavy barrier. Alas, those who wait for the cock to crow remain still within the murky depths of a drunken dream.
At the small assembly upon the conclusion of the retreat: dazed and vacant, muddled and clumsy; in the morning wandering to the Western Heaven, in the evening returning to this Eastern Land.
Vivid and distinct; precise and luminous. Having grasped the nostrils, they have lost the eyes.
Such two types of people are entirely without mutual interference. During these ninety days, they abide in this manner:
taking Perfect Enlightenment as their monastery, the One Vehicle as their gateway, Quiescent Extinction as their garden, and Wondrous Existence as their plaything. At this very moment:

Who is it that is so muddled and confused? Who is it that is so precise and lucid? A drop of water gives rise to ice; grass bends as the wind blows. This is fit to serve as a model for the monastic community.
Yet there is another person who does not accept established rules: his eyes look toward the southeast, while his mind dwells on the northwest.
Where, then, can he be placed? After a long silence, he said: "The heavy gates have once been thrown wide open; let the master enter."
"Returning to the Same Source. Jufenyang asked Shoushan about Baizhang’s "rolling up the mat. What was the meaning?

Shoushan said, "When the dragon’s sleeve is swept aside, the entire body is revealed. Jufenyang said, "What is your meaning, Master? Shoushan said, "Where the Elephant King walks, there is no trace of the fox.
Jufenyang said, "The moon in the empty expanse of the ten-thousand-year-old green pool—only after repeatedly searching for it can one truly know it. The Master said, "Shou..."
On level ground amidst the mountains, one can support and lift it up. Fenyang fished it out from dead water and, with his whisk, drew a line, saying:
"Setting aside the ancients for a moment, is there anyone who repays injustice with injustice?
He gave a shout.
Small-scale *chanshi* (private instruction) for the end of the summer retreat: Let go completely; there is not a single dharma that can be grasped by the mind.
When the seat is cleared away, even the slightest trace of thought is delusion. Proceeding thus, forever sever all conditions; internally, one is clearly and constantly aware.
Externally, it is cool and refreshing, used according to its own nature. Just consider these ninety days of secret practice and hidden application;

the clear seal and manifest tally—what can be avoided and what cannot—let that be for now. Holding up the whisk, he said: "This is that which this mountain monk has used throughout his life without exhausting it;
you all should know it thoroughly. Fortunately, because the cloth bag has been opened, I have no choice but to cast both hands away. He then threw it down.
The whisk-bearer said: "Suddenly remembering the green mountains, he returns; wishing to see the dusty world, he comes back down.
He raised the case of Senior Monk Ding, who asked Linji, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma?

Linji descended from his meditation seat, seized him, gave him a slap, and then pushed him away. Ding stood there motionless. A monk standing nearby said, "Senior Monk Ding, why do you not prostrate yourself?"

He prostrated himself. While performing his prostrations, he suddenly attained great enlightenment. The Master said, "The teaching style of Daji has been transmitted through four generations down to Linji.
Upon reaching this point, one must dismantle the household and scatter the estate. Layman Ding has attained awakening; tell me, did he gain the power of Linji or the power of the bystander?"
Small Assembly at Nengren Chan Monastery in Jiankang Prefecture;

Small Assembly on the Winter Solstice. Difficult, difficult! There is nowhere and no place from which to fix the gaze of the eyes. At the quiet night, the watchtowers strike the hours with their gongs and drums.
Every sound calls out to one another without concealment—how easy! A blink of an eye or a raise of an eyebrow is nothing but this.

Yet, though it is thus, it is still not so. If it is not so, who can suddenly perceive it? It is neither difficult nor easy; it is neither hard nor simple. The coiled dragon drinks from the clear mountain stream;
he knows only that the heavens are cold and people are cold, unaware that everyone is right here. Since we are already here...
[The Master] said, "In the end, it is cold for both heaven and man. After a long silence, he said, "Indeed, it is right here. He raised the case of two fellow practitioners under Linji.
One said, "Setting aside the capacities of the middle and lower grades, I ask my elder brother to speak a single phrase.
The other said, "As soon as you intend to ask, you have already missed it. [The first one] said, "If that is so, then I shall go and pay my respects to my elder brother. [The second one] said, "..."
This is a thief. The Master said: "The host within the guest; the guest within the host. The lion in its den, exchanging roars and growls.
How many people nowadays can truly recognize this?"

A Small Sermon on the Eve of the Year’s End. Before the thirtieth day of the twelfth lunar month, amidst bamboo doors and thatched windows where water drips and freezes, one should simply keep what is high level and what is low level.
After the thirtieth day of the twelfth lunar month, [one finds oneself] in the flowery avenues and willow-lined streets.
Harmonious breath is like the spring breeze; it does not hinder whether one rides a fat horse or a lean horse. It is precisely on the thirtieth day of the twelfth month:
the old year has already passed, and the new year has not yet arrived. Seizing the two ends, how can one communicate? After a long silence, he said:
The Taihu Lake spans thirty-six thousand mu; when the moon speaks from the heart of the waves, to whom does it speak?
A monk asked an ancient worthy, "What is it like when the year has ended and the age is exhausted? The worthy said, "As usual, the first month of spring is still cold."
The Master said: "Although these are but ordinary, commonplace words, you must not understand them as ordinary, commonplace words.
Only then can they be understood as ordinary, commonplace words. Do you understand? It is still cold in the early spring."
A Small Sermon for the Summer Retreat: A single phrase encompasses the three gates of mystery; each gate of mystery possesses three essential meanings.
I have shattered the whole lump and presented it for you to see. In the blink of an eye, white clouds stretch for thousands of miles. Tell me, what is this single phrase?
"Hai! In the place where 'the official will not admit even a needle,' the ancients mixed mud with water;
when there was 'private passage for carriages and horses,' they cut through iron and severed nails. This is the thoroughgoing, grandmotherly heart that exhausts one's primal vitality.
You ungrateful and unrighteous fellows—right inside the alms bowl, I scoop up a spoonful and pick up a chopstick. If you can bite through it and chew it to a pulp—*awk!* You thought and thought!"
"Originally, originally! What more need be said of one phrase or two phrases, or the gates of the Three Mysteries and Three Essentials?
*Du!* Such a view as this is like a drop of water that cannot even be digested. If you have not yet realized this, sit beneath the trees for the ninety days of summer retreat;

eventually, there will come a time when the moon shines clear. He cited Nanquan’s address to the assembly, saying: "Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra fought each other last night at the third watch; each person [received a blow]."
[The Master] gave him twenty blows and drove him out of the monastery. Zhaozhou stepped forward from the assembly and said, "Whom did the Master intend for the staff to strike?
Nanquan said, "Where does Old Wang’s fault lie? Zhaozhou then bowed. The Master said, "This is the medicinal formula that Old Wang experienced at the age of eighteen;
I have handed over the basket along with the medicine. If you can take a strong dose of it, it will surely [work]."
He took and replaced the crown bone.
At the Small General Assembly (Xiaosan) following the summer retreat: "An acre of land, three snakes and nine mice. When pressed together, water freezes into ice;
when split open, clouds disperse to reveal the moon. Deshan’s Small General Assembly—refusing to answer questions—is a majestic battle formation; capture and release lie within it.

I, Zhaozhou, offer this informal discourse (*xiaocan*) to provide a response. We shall grapple like horses before the master’s feet, with fists and kicks at our disposal. Nengren (the Buddha) answers when questioned and rests when there is no question.
I do not dare follow in the footsteps of those who came before, nor do I seek to conform to the habits of the present age.

For this entire summer, I have spent my time with two or three companions on wheat porridge and vegetable soup, making do with whatever was at hand. Let the ancient Buddhas and the pillars of the monastery do as they please.
Interpenetrating: A cat and a lantern converse together. Clouds over the South Mountain, rain on the North Mountain.

A person comes from East Zhejiang, yet goes off toward Jiangxi. Brightness and darkness, sharp and dull phrases—whether correct or biased, guest or host—look at them and they are all but idle furnishings.
Suddenly, someone says: "Can you call these 'idle furnishings'? He then raises his hand.
He said: "Shame, shame! It is simply that I have not yet dared to deceive you. He then cited Mazu.
A monk asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? Mazu said, "Come closer and I will tell you.
When the monk drew near, Mazu gave him a slap and said, "Six ears do not share a secret. Master Nanyuan Huanglong said:
The ancients still held that "six ears do not share a secret. Now, in various quarters, they gather five hundred or seven hundred disciples in a great clamor.
Disaster! Disaster! The Master said: "The pears of Zhengzhou and the dates of Qingzhou—those who know their sourness and sweetness should point them out to others.
Alas, these deluded words are muddled with deceit, making them all the more difficult to discern. When I first saw [this]..."
When he was thus brought up by him, he simply said, "I do not understand. One can be certain that the Elder of Longfeng would have been left utterly crestfallen.
Winter Solstice Small Sermon: It is not the wind-bell that rings; it is my own mind that rings. It is not the wind or the banner that move;

it is the mind of the worthy one that moves. To settle the case based on the facts—how marvelous! This is the unsurpassed heart-seal of the Patriarchs, the subtle life-gate of the patched-robed monks.
It has wandered through the monastic groves for over a thousand years. Since you call yourselves elite guests who investigate the profound, have you ever scrutinized it closely?
There is none. If you call this "meeting opportunity with opportunity" or "taking error for error," what connection does it have?

If you can cast your eye and take a look before forms or words have yet emerged—like a seal pressed upon space, where no traces are revealed—and if, at the very moment a question and answer arise, you are as swift as one covering their ears so that nothing can reach them—like a seal pressed upon water, where waves surge in competition—or if you can turn your body around...
He leans on his staff, turns his back, and reaches behind to pry it open. The yin is at its extreme and the yang is born; ice melts and walls crumble.
It is like a seal pressed into clay—not a hair’s breadth of deviation. Holding up his staff, he asks: "And what of this one seal? He strikes once and says:
"A generous thirty *ke* of candlelight for a night window; sitting alone on a *huchang*, investigate the source."
Zhaoqing was once meeting with Gushan. Zhaoqing said, "It is just a family meal. Gushan said, "How utterly insatiable you are!
Zhaoqing said, "Please be patient for a moment. Gushan said, "It is just a family meal. Zhaoqing said, "Furthermore, there is no fire today. Gushan said, "How utterly stingy you are!
Zhaoqing said, "Then simply take it away. The Master said: "A family meal and tea—how could they be something contrived? Gushan.

To strike once and come forth is improper; it is like jostling spoons and chopsticks, causing Langlang of Zhaoqing to be flustered and frantic. Closing doors and bracing gates, he attempts to ward it off but cannot discern it.
At Nengren Temple, they regard this as a matter of daily routine; at Taibi Linsheng, they claim it is not a matter of daily routine. This is extreme lack of contentment. Ultimately, how is it?
Can one cause it to be independent of family wealth and status? Wherein does true elegance reside?
A Small Lecture on Wearing Many Robes;
A Small Lecture for the Winter Solstice at Taiping Xingguo Chan Temple on Mount Jiang in Jiankang Prefecture.
The drumbeat has ceased its resonance, and the lamps and candles shine in mutual brilliance. Thus do I, the mountain monk, together with all you venerable seniors—so it is.
To meet face-to-face is the second head; to scatter sand and throw dirt is for the clever child to miss the mark.
Not meeting in this way is the third head; to splash water and splash mud is to set up a target and invite an arrow. In the ordinary course of daily life, there is no involvement with contrivance;
it is clearly and constantly known, functioning with a clear, cool autonomy. To call this "the solitary peak of Wondrous Mountain" is already to turn one's head and look back. Departing...

If one cannot even find the palace halls within the imperial city, how much less can one find them atop a distant peak? Walking slowly in meditation, standing shoulder-to-shoulder before the pavilions of the Jewel Mountain, they are all led away as a single group.
Do you, venerable elders, wish for the ultimate truth? The heavens are but an inch high; the earth is but a single scale-patterned expanse.
A single drop of water from the great ocean; the universe is but one person. If there are those who hear such words, they will immediately—

If you do not consent to go down, it will be just right for three thousand in the morning and eight hundred in the evening. If you still have not grasped this, you must by all means not move a muscle.
[The Master] cited the case where Yaoshan ordered ten Zen guests to escort Layman Pang.

As they were leaving, the Layman pointed to the snow in the air and said, "This fine snow falls flake by flake, never landing anywhere else. The Master then gave a shout. The guest Quan asked, "Where does it land? Thereupon, the Layman...

[Zhaozhou] gave him a slap. Xuedou’s full commentary says: "The layman must not act so carelessly. The layman said, "If you address me as a 'Chan guest' in this way, Old King Yama will not let you off.
Xuedou says: "Layman, what do you say? The layman gave him another slap and said, "To see with one's eyes yet be like one blind;
to speak with one's mouth yet be like one mute. The Master [Zhaozhou] said: "Overhead it is vast and boundless; beneath one's feet it is vast and boundless. To stand firm is—"

Easy to turn away from, yet difficult to pivot back toward. The Vajra-jewel sword strikes one with chilling cold; do not look outside the words of the critical pivot. Small retreat talk for the summer *pravāraṇā*:
Sitting in meditative repose within the monastery of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*), one abides in the wisdom of equality (*samatā-jñāna*).

The hornet does not cling to its old nest; how could a dragon lie dormant in stagnant water? To go forth in this very way is to turn the body upon level ground and take slow steps at the tip of the fishing pole.
Where there is stability and solidity, there is no hindrance to the treacherous and precipitous; within the treacherous and precipitous, there is naturally stability and solidity.
Carrying out and carrying in, let it be as you please to deliberate. As for Letting the Patriarch Go—what is Master Ma?
As for Deshan and Wood Seat Monk, or Linji and the Vajra King—how would you explain them? He lets out a shout: "The Iron-Wheel Emperor issues his decree throughout the realm! The Innkeeper’s House!"
The wind, too, is uniquely its own. To cite a verse by Layman Pang: "The ten directions gather together; each and every one studies non-action. This is the field for selecting Buddhas;
with an empty mind, they return as top graduates. The Master said: "Layman Pang was indeed capable of restraining himself to benefit others. At the beginning..."
Where is the one who dwells as a companion to the myriad dharmas? If you can discern this, who will ascend the field of selecting Buddhas?
If none are thus, then I grant that one whose mind is empty has passed the examination.

Small-scale *chanshi* (private instruction) upon the conclusion of the summer retreat: Body and mind are as one; there is nothing beyond the body. It is like a stone containing jade, or a deep pool concealing pearls.
If this is so, then the rustling green bamboos skillfully perform the verses for ascending the hall when welcoming the breeze;
every drop of dew upon the lotus flowers fully reveals the pivot of entering the room. Thus, throughout this summer, my mouth remained hanging on the wall—this is merely a brief summary.
One attains the ultimate matter; there is no such thing as passing through it empty-handed rather than empty-handed. Suddenly, someone comes forth and says: "Poverty last year was not yet poverty;
poverty this year is only then poverty. When the meaning arrives, it is not as good as when the phrase arrives. What is it like to have eyes that are intimate compared to hands that are intimate?
One must not yet be buried alive on the shore of dead water. *Agha!* I have heard these words in the past; today I joyfully see the person who embodies them.
Master Sida was engaged in summer retreat meditation, sitting with a majestic stillness that remained unmoving.

At the conclusion of the summer retreat, an attendant monk said, "Today is the day of *pravāraṇā*. The Master sighed and said, "During the Buddha’s lifetime, those who realized the Way were countless.
Now that the Sage has long been gone, we have attained nothing at all. As he lay down and relaxed his body, his faculty of sight suddenly became pure, and he saw everything clearly.
The three thousandfold world-system is like looking at the palm of one’s hand. The Master’s verse says:

"When reclining amidst the sound of sighs and lamentations, the grasses of the three thousand worlds grow lush and tall. He picks up his staff and strikes once, saying: "If only this old fellow had clarified this principle!"
The nostrils have always hung downward.
On this New Year’s Eve small *chan* lecture: profound, firm, remote, and deep; only those who arrive know it. Exposed and revealed before one's eyes, there is no action that is not so.
Time and again, they sleep through the long night of birth and death, never once awakening. What will happen on the thirtieth day of the twelfth month?
I recall how Master Zihu, in the middle of the night within the monks' hall, called out in a loud voice: "Thieves! Thieves!"
The Master said, "A reed arrow! The assembly was startled and rose. The Master said, "It has already passed through. He then seized a monk and said, "Caught!
Caught! The Master said, "Wait, wait. The monk said, "It was not I.
The Master said, "Offered up but not becoming a dragon. Huo said, "It is so, it is so; it is simply that he is unwilling to accept responsibility. The Master said, "In the center."
"Nine down, seven. This old fellow beats the drum upon the elephant-hide mat until the people of the entire world have their eyes trembling to this very day.
It is simply that the evidence is incomplete; he has evaded it right before our faces. He might as well be let off. Today is the thirtieth day of the twelfth month;
at night we dare not touch him. We shall wait for his dreams to grow deep; then, without being caught, he will be defeated of himself. Thus it is said.
"Thirty blows! Why? A blink of an eye is already next year.
The Master cites a monk who asked Zhaozhou, "I have newly entered the monastery; I beg the Master for instruction. Zhaozhou said, "Have you finished eating your congee?
The monk replied, "I have finished eating my congee. Zhaozhou said, "Go wash your bowl. The Master says: "Just so—cite it thus."
Once, while making offerings to the great assembly late at night when all was silent and there was no one to rely upon, I tried turning it over and looking at it from every side;
suddenly, I struck upon it. Now, I beg you for a word of instruction.
A Small Sermon for the Summer Retreat. Holding up his staff, he said: "Right like this—when the manifest style is encountered, it becomes a perilous fall.
Not right like this—when held in the back of the hand, it must be scrutinized again. Both right like this—a single phrase of *upāya* unites self and other.
Neither right like this—who dares to blunt its sharp edge when it is brought forth? A-ha-ha! Who will take up the burden? When refined gold of a hundred smeltings meets [the fire]..."
A blazing fire! Opening the heavy gates and removing the double locks, light and darkness are simultaneously rent asunder.
When one gazes with bated breath toward the south, north, east, and west, a horned tiger sits vaguely upon the threshold. *He lets out a shout.*
Fengxue was brought before Nanyuan. Nanyuan asked, "Upon entering the gate, one must distinguish the master. Fengxue said, "I ask the Master to distinguish this with a single phrase.
Nanyuan struck his knee with his left hand; Fengxue then gave a shout. Nanyuan struck his knee with his right hand; Fengxue also gave a shout.
Nanyuan raised his left hand and said, "This one, let us leave to you, Dharma brother. He then raised his right hand and said, "As for this one, what about it? Fengxue— [gave a shout].
"Blind! Yunmen said. Xuefeng then picked up his staff. Yunmen asked, "What are you doing? Seizing the staff, Xuefeng struck him, saying, "Tell the Master not to say I didn't warn you.
Yunmen threw down the staff and said, "Today I have been thoroughly outwitted by this yellow-faced man from Zhejiang."

Xiang. A Universal Discourse on the Incense Offering at Jiangshan.
The divine light is never obscured; it is a magnificent legacy for all ages. Upon entering this gate, do not harbor notions of knowledge or understanding.
How marvelous! The ancients fashioned a mold that has been so revealed, so clarified, so direct, and so intimate.
If one could see it upon the very first glance, why go through all this—forming ranks and arrays, advancing and retreating, and just barely gaining entry?
As for those in the monastic forests, they truly do not know the beginning or the end. As for those who have practiced for a long time, how should they act? Do you still understand?
When I, this mountain monk, speak of "clarity," it is already obscured; when I speak of "manifestation," it is already covered over;
when I speak of "simplicity," it is already prolix; when I speak of "intimacy," it is already circuitous and remote.
It is understood. How can one avoid this fault? This Dharma-seal of mine pervades all places without any deficiency;
it pervades all times without interruption. Tell me, can you obscure it? Can you cover it over? Can you bypass it?
If you wish to be intimate with it, first of all, do not seek it within the physical heart.
Above all, one falsely discriminates, falsely creates intimacy and distance, falsely posits self and other, and falsely contends over victory and defeat.
As soon as one acts in this way, one misses the mark. As soon as one lets go, there is vast openness, empty fusion, serenity, and tranquil ease.

When encountering circumstances and conditions, one acts spontaneously and perfectly. At this point, even the slightest trace of a hair’s breadth is defilement; how much more so is deliberate conceptualization?
Discriminating between self and others, victory and defeat, they harbor crafty and hypocritical minds while hoping for the wondrous Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
Such people are truly to be pitied. Among them is a certain group of brothers who, upon seeing an elder ascend the hall or enter the room, do nothing but pick up what he says offhand;

Alas! Why do you not melt away the notions of self and other, right and wrong, to become Prajñā? Now, instead, you turn Prajñā back into self and other, right and wrong.
It is like the supreme flavor of *amṛta* (clarified butter), which is prized by the world; yet when encountered by such people as these, it turns instead into a poisonous drug.
Now, let us speak with earnest precision: simply recognize that which is not [the self] within a single thought-moment and let it all go from the very bottom.

If you briefly turn the light back upon itself, you will immediately be identical to what was originally attained. All prior discursive thinking and discrimination, along with the notions of self and other, victory and defeat, will simultaneously be extinguished.
Have you ever yet reached such a state? Even if you were to reach it, it would still be "not yet. Why do you not urgently knock at every door and enter every house to seek it?

A decisive severance. Have you not seen? Formerly, there was a bhikṣu who said to the Buddha, "Within the Dharma of the World-Honored One, my place of realization is correct, yet my place of verification is not yet so.
What will the World-Honored One show me? The Buddha called out, "Bhikṣu So-and-so! [The bhikṣu replied,] "What will you show me?

If one says it is not difficult, then since the time of the picking of the flower and the smile until Caoxi, barely seventeen hundred years have passed.
In terms of such time, all people throughout the entire world have long been universally urged to become Buddhas. How then can anyone [claim otherwise]?
The transmission was passed to a single person, continuing without interruption like a thread. Once the barriers of Caoxi were breached, both the teachings and the realization were fully realized.

In Jiangxi, the path underwent a transformation where both the fundamental principle and its functional application were raised together; through secret resonance and manifest correspondence, those who possessed the great eye of wisdom became countless.
Now another five hundred years have passed. Today, [the Dharma] is being lost on all sides to such an extent.

If one speaks of this matter, only those of the highest capacity (*agradhātu*) are capable of bearing it; those of middling or inferior capacity have no share in it. As for those of the highest capacity—who indeed are they?

As it is said: "Externally cease all conditions; internally let the mind be without panting. Let the mind be like a wall, and only then can one enter the Way. This, too, was illustrated by Shaolin.

Master Yantou called it the "Culminating Phrase," the "Correct Position," and "Attaining Abiding. Beginners and new students do not recognize this phrase.

Wuyi, you have failed to escape the passage of time and have wandered aimlessly, abandoning your home and losing your livelihood. Suddenly, a pang of compassion arose within you as you realized your error;

yet though you tried to rise up, you could not do so all at once. It was as if scraped by a blade and washed away by water, yet a lingering unease remained in your heart—half-remembered, half-forgotten—as your failures grew ever more profound.
Master Yuan, you have traveled south from a dream-like state, seeking a single phrase to aid your awakening. I...
One wishes to lift Mount Sumeru as a mallet and strike the drum of empty space;

yet fearing one cannot summon it, for sleep has not yet fully ended and the urge to depart is uncontrollable—at the moment of piercing the clouds and crossing the waters, if one loses one's footing while walking with steady steps, the eye will open of its own accord.
Only at this time may one explore the tiger’s den of the Southern Mountain and penetrate the dragon gate of the Eel Well. First, fix your resolve upon him.
Do not allow it to turn or roll over; only then may you pull its claws and teeth and toy with its head and horns.
Otherwise, if it delivers a single bite, your entire life will be lost. Though this may be called a virtuous cause, it brings about an evil result.
Attendant Shiyuan, in the past,
when Yaoshan went to seek the Way at Mount Nanyue, he first heard the words, "Neither 'thus' nor 'not thus' are both permissible," which were like a mosquito trying to bite an iron ox.
When he reached the point where "nothing is done," and "sitting idly is the doing," it was as if he were upon the water.
The gourd. Though you press it, you cannot press it down; though the skin continues to peel away, you do not realize that the reality still remains.
This has led those who drift with the waves to say, "I have been at Yaoshan for thirty years, clarifying this matter alone.
When sowing grain, beans instead grow. Try to examine it: where exactly does his failure lie?
The nine ascending stages and the three arrivals have reached their limit; the bottom of the bucket has been knocked off, yet it remains in the hands of the wooden patriarch.
Why, then, does he linger at the Āoshān Inn, mired in the shell of delusion?

In the middle of the night, hearing Master Huō strike the "poison-painted" drum, he causes Yanguan’s doctrine of form and emptiness and Dōngshān’s verse on crossing the water to shake the earth and radiate light. This was because Cēngláng had long engaged in the practice of arrogance.
Is it not a fault?
The First Patriarch of India called to the Second Patriarch and said, "Throw down the banner pole in front of the gate! He opened it wide with eight strokes and handed it over with both hands.
Why? Yongquan said, "Even after forty years, I still have a tendency toward conceptual movement. Xianglin said: [The rest of the passage follows].
For forty years, I have finally forged them into a single piece.
Without leaving Feiyuan Ridge, my gaze pierces the nine heavens; without descending Mount Diaoyu, my spirit swallows the four seas.

Master Bei and Master Hui—though from different eras and distant lands—I pass them all through with a single document. As for that fellow who, at eighteen, broke up his home and scattered his household—why is this?
To tire yourself out without ceasing—will this not merely be a waste of straw sandals? If you say that the misty waters of a hundred cities mean "where do you go?
and "where do you come from," or that ten thousand miles of mountains and rivers are simply "underfoot"—I fear these are precisely the points where one goes astray.
He speaks of Chan with great flourish; yet do you know the news of those who "plow the fields and trade for their meals"?

Do those who plow the fields and trade for their meals know the principle of him who speaks of Chan with such flourish? If one does not let go with ease, how could there be anything less than one principle or two meanings?
Attendant Pujiangyuan requested a phrase to take back to his hometown; thus, five pieces of dried tangerine peel were given.

I present this fragment as a gift. Upon returning to your mountain home, you must strictly avoid chewing upon it; not only will it be flavorless, but it will also scrub away the impurities from within your breast.
This is shown to Chan Master Yuan.
At the top of a hundred-foot pole, beyond the mountain stream bridge, the donkey stumbled and its own eyes suddenly opened. Thereupon he spoke a verse:
"I have a bright pearl, Long confined by the dust of worldly toil. Now that the dust is cleared and the light shines forth, It pierces through ten thousand peaks of the green mountains.
Alas! Where has the Master of Mount Yú from Táchéng gone? He was one who constantly shook his bells and rang his gongs.

When trilling the tongue to produce the *brahman* sound, is this not the bright pearl emitting its light? When the hand falters and the foot slips, within the sound of "A-di," one's true face is fully revealed.
To have two heads or three heads—how much later would that be! Master Yuan was well able to investigate and examine this minutely;
between the past and the present, there is no space even for a hair. Nevertheless, in all places, take the direct mind as [the standard].
In the place of practice (*bodhimaṇḍa*), one acts as a Buddha directly; one speaks of true repentance directly; one employs skillful empowerment directly.
Otherwise, one deceives oneself with delusions, which neither Buddhas nor Patriarchs will accept. To speak of other matters as having merit is not something I can know;
to claim such knowledge would be mere empty chatter upon empty chatter, which cannot avoid being the object of a smile from Chaling.
He showed the meaning of my teaching to Attendant Che:
it is like a poison-smeared drum; when struck once, everyone within hearing range, whether far or near, perishes. That those who hear it perish is certainly so, but what of the deaf?
Xuefeng asked Deshan: "Regarding the matters of the ancestral school, how are they transmitted?"

Shanshan struck him once with his staff and asked, "What do you say? The next day, Xuefeng requested further instruction. Deshan said, "In my school there are no words or phrases, nor is there a single dharma given to anyone.
Upon hearing this, Master Cunen felt a sudden clarity within his breast, as if the bottom had fallen out of a bucket.
As for other great masters of the lineage who displayed a single pivot or uttered a single word, there were those who, upon hearing them, became deaf, and those who, upon seeing them, [became blind].
They may protrude their tongues; they may clap their hands and laugh; they may wave their hands; they may lurch their bodies as they run;
or they may bend both knees of their own accord—all these are those who have perished amidst the sound of the drum.

This is for no other reason than that their will and spirit are perfectly aligned, their mental focus is single-minded, and in every place and situation, they are able to let go with their whole being, take up responsibility with their whole being, and roll up and unfold with their whole being.
The whole body experiences it as if standing upon the summit of Mount Sumeru with one’s head facing downward; except that these eyes do not yet open.
Once the eyes open, then to the left, right, before, and behind—the four great continents, the sun, moon, and stars, the mountains, rivers, and the great earth—all appear.
All these are but a single thing beneath my heels. If your standing place is not high, you cannot avoid the distinctions of near and far, high and low;
you will wander aimlessly back and forth, falling upon crossroads with no end in sight.

How much more so for those of superior character, who possess the true cause and perfect faith, who prepare their superior body and mind, and attend upon superior teachers and friends—how could they ever waste their years and months?
Fearing that what was undertaken would not be accomplished, he did not join the great elders of former generations in this matter.

Whether it be "three clear and two dark," or "half before and two after," they prattle on and chatter incessantly, floundering in confusion within a bag of antiques, emerging from one head only to plunge back in another.
If one hopes for a single moment of resonance with the truth, then even if there are a hundred sounds of poisoned lacquer, they can do nothing at all.
To speak in such a manner is to have a second head; to believe such a statement is to lose a third head. Or, upon hearing it, it is like the wind passing over the treetops.
It is like pouring water on a stubborn stone. I believe this person has already realized this samādhi under the Buddha Empty King;
how could it be easily attained? The attendant Liaochè of Fucheng has long been within the assembly at Beishan, preparing for this Way.
He sought words from the Western City to serve as a warning and aid. Thus it is said:
"To the practitioner who contemplates mindfulness:
It is not the wind-bell that rings; it is my own mind that rings. It is not the wind or the banner that move; it is your own mind, O worthy one, that moves. How marvelous!
This is the staff of the Indian and Chinese patriarchs, which strikes the grass to startle the snake. Have you ever washed your ears and rubbed your eyes within its midst? (2)
A thousand years ago, a hundred thousand *li* away—all is present right now. Every step I take, every place my feet touch, is my own mountain-home.
What strikes my ears and dazzles my eyes is my very self. Hundreds, thousands, tens of millions—these are all my kinsmen.
Those fifty-two or fifty-three [years] are but a single acquaintance. From the outset, there was no distinction between China and India; how could there be any separation between Wu and Shu?

How different this arrival is! To pause and look about, one sees that the Chinese are simply the Chinese, and the Indian (Zhū) are simply the Indian. The mountains, rivers, winds, and scenery are distinct in every direction;
the markets, streets, pavilions, and towers stand tall and imposing at every turn. A gentle breeze rustles through the trees, causing the banners to flutter and the bells to chime.
What is seen by the eyes and heard by the ears cannot be concealed even by a thousand hands. At such a time, there is not the slightest possibility of deceiving him. Did not the former sage say:
"I now act as a guarantor for you regarding this matter; it shall never be in vain"? I, Nian, have accompanied my venerable teacher back to his home village.
I imagine he will no longer suffer the toil of patting one’s back [in consolation]. Thus, I have joyfully written this to present to him as a gift.

The practitioner Shen is a monk among the assembly at Beishan. He frequently visits Xicheng to inquire after my well-being in my solitude.
One day, he was about to return home in high spirits when he suddenly came to bid me farewell. It happened that I had ascended the Zhengchuan Pavilion on Beishan to read ancient texts.
During the Sui dynasty, Guizhi verified the tortoise at the Wooden Meditation Hut; Lao Xianglin verified the tortoise at the Crystal Palace.

"When the great chiliocosm perishes, he departs with it"—such words as "burning the mountains in the twelfth month" resound through heaven and earth, their radiance illuminating both past and present, impossible to suppress.
Alas! Their skillful means were no match for the model of the [Northern] school. These two elders, however, took up the Southern School and traced its course back to the West.

then, from morning in Eastern Wu to evening in Western Shu, the myriad forms of mountains and rivers and the wind and moon shall become one family. With the staff in hand, let nothing pass in vain.
May those who practice deep Chan exert themselves!
To show that this Dharma is not something that can be understood through deliberation or conceptual discrimination: O guests who investigate the profound mystery, what do you call "this Dharma"?
Here, utter a turning word that cuts off the tongues of all past and present, so that no one falls into the trap of thought.
One can fully understand all conceptualizations and discriminations; yet, should one hesitate even slightly, one will merely dream within the realm of thought and discrimination. As Guishan said:
"By means of the wondrous state where there is no thinking through thinking, one returns to the contemplation of the infinite, spiritual flame. When thinking is exhausted, one returns to the source;
nature and characteristics are equal, principle and phenomena are non-dual—the true Buddha is suchness. This is a profound discourse on entering into principle; it is not otherwise.
Without Mount Gui, what could he call "the true Buddha"? Does the Buddha have a false aspect?

Furthermore, what kind of turning word (*vākya*) could be applied here to prevent the entanglement of nature and characteristics, principle and phenomena, thought and non-thought, into a single mass from which there is no way out? Otherwise, look further at the complications of Yangshan:

to know through thought is to fall into the second head; not to think— *Note: The text provided ends abruptly. To "know" is to fall into the third category. To transcend categories and differ from the eye—this is not without precedent in the case of Yangshan.
Yet, even if one thinks and knows, what exactly does one know? What kind of turning word can be applied here to avoid falling into the duality of "two heads" and "three categories"?
The official will not allow even a needle to pass. To repay his kindness, he heads toward the tangled vines; there, the branches and tendrils proliferate. To think about it is to cloud one's vision;

Among the practitioners of our school, none have been able to penetrate its net; how much less so a single golden rooster or a single colt?

Among those who have since settled within the monastic groves, nine out of ten remain oblivious throughout their lives, unaware of [the truth]; or they know it but do not practice; or they practice but fail to reach its ultimate realization.
Thus, the ancestral temple falls into decay and the lineage’s foundation lies desolate. This was once a grove of sandalwood...
The groves were once gardens of ambrosia, yet now thorns pierce the sky and foxes and rabbits cross their paths.
Is this not the fault of those who sit upon curved wooden couches, presiding over the Great Dharma? Or is it the fault of those who leave one forest only to enter another?

the meditation cushions and Zen boards are everywhere among good friends, and the "hemp thorns" and "golden circles" are at all times a delicious flavor. Master.

Sometimes he snaps his staff in two; sometimes he picks up a winnowing fan. Ten thousand ages of mountains and rivers, a single morning’s wind and moon—stepping on them at every turn, meeting "Him" (the Buddha-nature) everywhere.

If high-minded practitioners of the pilgrimage do not take the ancient sages as their standard, nor do they strike at their own true nature in earnest practice, they are called blind.

In studying the Way, I have no special talent; it is simply that my resolve has not failed. This is true of all who study this Way—why should it be unique to my late teacher?

Regarding the story of the attendant Shixin: Formerly, when Master Ze was serving as the Prior for King Li, he ascended the hall. A monk asked, "The dragon roars and the mist gathers; the tiger shouts and the wind arises. The student knows these are matters pertaining to the transcendence of the world, yet why do I not understand? Ze said, "Understand it well! His attendant, Shixin, was present at that time. Later, he asked Ze, "What did you mean by saying, 'Understand it well'? Ze replied, "I meant that you should understand that the dragon's roar and the tiger's shout are both within your own mind. Shixin then asked, "If they are within my own mind, how can I understand them? Ze said, "If you could understand them, they would no longer be within your own mind. Shixin attained great enlightenment upon hearing this. He subsequently composed a verse to express his realization: "The dragon roars and the mist gathers; The tiger shouts and the wind arises. When the sound is heard, the form is seen; When the form is seen, the sound is heard. The sound and form are both within my own mind; Why then do I not understand? If I were to understand, They would no longer be within my own mind. Later, he served as the Abbot of Mount Jingci. One day, while ascending the hall, he addressed the assembly, saying: "The dragon roars and the mist gathers; the tiger shouts and the wind arises. At that moment, the entire assembly attained great enlightenment. This is recorded in the *Jingde Chuandeng Lu*.
