The wind is still in the level forest; the clouds are light in the valley coves. A single scoop of cold spring water offers tribute to the traveler’s heart. I shall surely make another appointment with this mountain;
why not practice walking meditation here once every day?
I bid farewell to Minister Yang with this painting of ten-thousand-li rivers and mountains; it records his return on the brocade sails and his promise to come again.
It would be well to add, amidst the misty clouds and vapors, a fluttering imperial messenger urging him forward.

In praise of the integrity and virtue of the late State Historian Yi’s ancestors, the Elder and his younger brothers: Their solemn presence stood side by side in the Sage Dynasty; From father to son, and from grandson to grandson, they followed in succession.
As this old monk counts them on my fingers, the day will not be far off.
To the Magistrate Shangyuan:
Holding up a single word, Zhaozhou’s “No” is not even equal to a three-foot blade. It severs all myriad distinctions at once;
even the white clouds dare not trespass upon its pure emptiness.
Seeing off Prefect Zhao Fengtai in the Fifth Month:
Cold clouds do not fly, remaining damp and heavy. At the moment of parting, there are no words, only lingering thoughts. This heart shall not be separated by mountains and rivers;
From time to time, I shall listen for the sound of his carriage as it approaches my bamboo gate.
Master Sun clearly knows that his study of learning benefits him daily; yet he does not know how it would be if he were practicing the Way.
He merely feels that his family is poor and his body is gradually aging, and that his intelligence is no longer as sharp as it once was.
Sending off Elder Mo to enter Zhejiang: Where there is a Buddha, do not dwell;
strike the coral tree with an iron whip until it shatters. Where there is no Buddha, pass by in haste;
do not allow the azure dragon to lie within the clear depths. Three thousand miles away, do not err in your raising [of the whisk]. Raising the eyebrows, the eyes stand firm and piercing.
If it is so, then one does not go. The misty waters of a hundred cities are difficult to depict. Plucking the willow flowers—plucking the willow flowers.
Before you can even blink, you have already forgotten your home. Zhaozhou’s tongue hangs suspended for a thousand days; like a spark of stone or a flash of lightning, it cannot be pursued.
When the paper lamp is blown out, one knows where one returns; it falls upon the second pivot of my house.

Turning over and grasping the black staff upside down, one refuses to dwell within the net of the thousand sages. When will you grind and polish to stem the surging waves? With a great fan of true wind, fill the entire universe.
Sending off Jizhao-an to return to Shu:
It is still tolerable that he came south by mistake; but once he has returned home, a mistake is difficult to rectify.
Indeed, in the end, he is taken away by his error; thirty-six rivers all flow toward the west.
The mountain stream elder knew the handle of the dipper grew long as the waters receded; from this point on, the family tradition turned desolate. Sometimes waves rise where there is no wind;
one looks coldly upon those who cut across the current, busily occupied with themselves.
The ox-hide robe is the life-vein of the monk and the eye atop the crown of the head; once touched, horns emerge without cause. Fortunately, the home garden and fields are secure;
where one can plow deeply, one should plow deeply.

On a moonless night, Master He was rowing his boat past Xi-xi Lake with Layman Xie. Unaware that he had drifted to rest against the bank of the Yan River, he used a single pole at hand to pivot the craft around.
The whole family washed their feet and went up to bed to sleep.
Sending off the Chan practitioner of Jinzhou:
The Great Being’s eyes are squinting from grinding bricks. Go back and call him awake with a loud voice. What a fine message for striking the cart!
It was pointlessly entrusted to a foal.
Sent to the Chan practitioner Hui of Dazhou: Look at the face of Wuzhun of Mount Jing;
his eyes are turned inward and the sinews are twisted upward. Of all Buddhas, who is the primary body? When you go there, offer incense and perform three prostrations, then rise;
guard against those who speak left-handed words and fan others into delusion.
The Sword Hall usually does not reveal its sharp edge; its frosty majesty is naturally complete. Before even stepping through the gate, one must be on guard;
who knows that [the sword] has already struck the skull?
In Wuyin and Wangzhou, we have not yet met; at Nanyue and Tiantai, we have conversed many times.
This has led to Mount Lu losing its smile, leaving my face full of shame to this very day.
Seeing off a Monk Crossing Mount Jin (after the death of Yanshi Hui):
I do not see De-yun, the idle old cypress; Faint smoke and cold sun reflect upon the ripples of the water. The wind blows and thunder rolls upon the distant peaks;
It would be well to bow one’s head and pay him one’s respects.
Without illumination, one pities oneself; not a single speck is polished away. Opening the eyes is no different from passing through them closed. Do not say the whole family is completely muddled;
see what happens when you try to deceive him by even a little.
The Clear Stream is but a few feet away; the road to Cao’s Source is open. Why do the swimming fish lose their way? When they encounter an uneven place, they make a sound;
not even a speck of dust or mud can find entry.

Sending forth the mind, neither the hut nor this—this is a golden fish still lingering in the water. Neither "is" nor "is not"—the lion turns its body once more. Beyond "is" and "is not" lies the excellence of the mountains of Shu;
who can rely upon for the mastery of the Buddha-dharma?
The moon-lake is bright and pure, its clear light shimmering with cold radiance. How many times have I stirred the waves in my search?
Who can tell this to Hanshan? Do not view my mind as being the same as yours.
Without form, tranquil, empty, and at ease, before a single line has moved—what single or split lines, what double or intersecting lines could there be? In an age of Great Peace, it should be thus;
when meeting people, do not cast the hexagram haphazardly.
Sending off the monk to Zhedong:
a single patch of ground where one cannot tread. It is as rotten as raw iron and as hard as mud.
Having searched everywhere in Jinling without finding a trace, it must surely lie on the eastern ridge of Mount Maofeng.
Seeing the old man Beijian fall over while escorting a monk past Biyun, Yangqi’s brain was missing from his skull.
Who can discuss his conduct in action or retirement? At the depths of Biyun, I ask for the ultimate truth:
he is the ninth-generation descendant of that very house.

The snow ox stands out clearly in the vast expanse, unable to be driven away; from time to time it wanders through the deep village and the wild weeds. Its coat and hide have been entirely transformed;
such a being alone is fit to bear the burden.
The iron walls and the heavens and earth serve as a furnace for smelting; that which is impenetrable allows the wind to pass through.
Since returning after having penetrated this, one sees layer upon layer.

Sending off the venerable masters Yin and Yi to return to the south of Shu, they traveled by circuitous routes seeking out the Westward Transmission. Their mouths wished to speak, yet the words would not open;
Yi’s horse and Yin’s staff were taken away. By the stream, the old woman laughed heartily.

The stone gate is locked by clouds and sealed by moss; its terrain is steep and perilous. There too, one has spent blows with the wheel-hammer. It is simply because of that place where one cannot enter;
there, the workings of the mind are forgotten and the path is cut off.

Seeing that there is nothing to know, the smoke and water of a hundred cities are cold with night-light; I once gazed closely at the top of Jizifeng Peak. When the body is turned around, the sky has already dawned;
what one gains before the eyes is a vast, dark expanse.
As the Venerable Xiang proceeds to his place of practice, his tiger-staff soars high toward Tiger Rock. At Tiger Rock, the tiger’s breath is fierce and imposing;
though he hides the "Father-and-Son" hands of Jibei in his sleeve, he cannot bear it without stroking its whiskers.

The place where Master Puo remains hidden and preserves his true nature is when the浑仑 (the primordial whole) has not yet been split open. From the beginning it has always been thus; there is no need to search for flaws.
Sent to the Monk Wu as he enters Guangzhou, also addressed to Tu, the Circuit Intendant.
The great earth is like a single grain of millet; to whom now is this teaching entrusted? From time to time, grasp it in the palm of your hand and look:
the mountains and rivers of Wu and Shu are as fresh as ever.
On the Snowy Mountains, day is vast and night is vast; high peaks and low ridges are all one and the same.
When the body dwells within this luminous clarity, do not look from within that clarity.
The title of Magistrate Peng remains as before:
Han Ben has never had a face. For years he has wandered aimlessly toward the external world; suddenly remembering, he returns home.
Six times six remain as they were: thirty-six.
The Jade Attendant has appeared in the world at the Deer Park;
the ocean of practice is windless, and the moon of precepts stands solitary. The new opening of the Deer Park follows the old model;
among the seventeen hundred who have transmitted the lamp, is there anyone who clearly sees the pattern?
The stone mirror is firm and stubborn; how could it have been cast? Washed by rain and polished by wind, it remains just as it is. Do not say that it does not illuminate at all;
the mountain spirits’ hearts have already burst, leaving nothing behind.
The indolent monk’s cold tears stream down his chin, too weary to wipe them away; he refuses to hang the Buddha-dharma upon his mind. He has cast aside even his needle-case and thread-bag;
let the ancient rags rot and fall apart as they please.
Seeing Master Jue off as he returns to Longxing:
Among eighty-four men of virtue and wisdom, Master Liang walked hand-in-hand with him, yet they did not return together. I know your home is up in Jiangxi;
cease listening to the sound of the rapids and their idle disputes.
"Where do you, Master from the South, reside? What is your name? He remained silent and did not answer, smiling with serene joy. "I know you are no one who has come from the North;
you have brought down the pure breeze, which you surely know yourself."
A skilled Chan practitioner ascended Mount Jing to attend Chijue for three years;
though they lived together, they did not recognize one another. His eyebrows and eyes were wide-set, his nose long and straight. Meeting him on a narrow path, where was he bound?
He wished to ascend to the summit of Mount Lingxiao. One peak of Lingxiao thrusts high into the heavens; the other peaks rise and fall around it.
My children, I have once gazed with eyes that could discern a fine hair at autumn’s end; the three thousand oceans of lands are but empty toil.

The Old Man of the Peak Peak is eighty-two years old; his deep-set eyes reflect the waters of autumn. His laughter, jests, scoldings, and rebukes, even the sound of his coughing—all these are the primary truth of our house.
The Old Man asks you: from where have you come? Step forward and place your hands together across your chest. Look further still!
The martial gait gives rise to a pure breeze; why worry that the old man has no smile?

In the absence of contention, the picking up of the flower and the smile gave rise to strife; facing the wall to settle the mind, the marketplace was laid open. Counting on back to old Lu, the supreme clarity is revealed.
Seated, he causes the human consciousness to become suddenly ashen.
Sending this to the venerable Master He of Japan:

"Last night, my returning dream wandered through the passes of my homeland; how could the vast blue sea ever obstruct one's coming and going? To those who ask of the Son of Heaven of the Great Tang: [I am here].
The Master said, "To perceive Tuṣita residing in the human realm:

its flavor is as sweet as licorice yet slightly tinged with bitterness, like yellow myrobalan; it is as bitter as licorice yet faintly carries a pungency. Each time one tastes it, it becomes more so."
Separate! I only fear it will be difficult to deceive the tongueless one.
At Fangyan, black clouds gather, then white clouds gather; as the clouds withdraw, the ridges divide in four directions. The level and the precipitous both rest within.
Severed. Moreover, there were no falling rains of flowers.

Sending off the monk to the Twin Trees (Śāla Grove), upon arriving at the Twin Trees he beheld his former companion: eyebrows curved like the new moon, eyes spanning the autumn sky. Before even a word of greeting could be exchanged, one should first—
Question: Why does the bridge flow while the water does not?
The flawless fundamental substance is as warm and as luminous as crystal. To attempt to carve it with the mind is a waste of effort; one’s own precious treasury is simply this.
This is so. By all means, do not scrub or stain this channel.
I have sent the guest prefect of Zhen a plot of old farmland in Hainan; the pines and bamboos welcome the breeze—how pitiable they are! I wipe away the wisteria vines and lean against my bed.
Bàn. Regarding the question of the Patriarchal Chan asked by the people of the embankments:
"A letter from Jiangxi was received at Mount Jingshan;

it had been hidden in the mountains for five hundred years, and has now been sent to Xian of Sagami. ○ [Seal] Sagami Shogun. ○ [Seal] Mount Jingshan. [Seal] Received the news from Jiangxi. Hidden in the mountains for five hundred years. Transmitted to Xian of Sagami.
The Prefect: "There is no need for me to point out flaws; let things be as they naturally are.

I see the gentleman Ding departing in his rosy robes and cloud-crowned cap to roam the Imperial Gardens. With straw sandals and bamboo staff, he passes through secluded gates; on his old mountain, the green grass grows in profusion.
At the tomb: "I am ashamed to see the Master return as a crane from his transformation.

In the stillness of a narrow window, I have transcribed the Lotus Sūtra with my own blood. One character, one dot—all is blood. When the blood is exhausted and the brush worn away, I say: 'Stop, stop; there is no need to speak.'"

Opening up various dialects to gather fallen blossoms and affix them to old branches—wandering bees and dancing butterflies fly about in vain confusion. Do not let them sniff where there is no fragrance;
they will only return by the old path with their faces cast down in shame.
A small tuft of natural hair atop the crown of the head— though shaved, it grows back and will not cease. When the golden razor catches it at an angle,
every single hair remains exactly as it was.
The practitioner Deshan changed his name to Dezhi;

he was the sole virtue of our school. For several hundred years, the world has looked up to him with one mind. Through the vast silence of time, the pure breeze of his legacy has continued to blow without ceasing.
Your name now shares the same character; at first, it was not a violation of his taboo. Yet when called out before others, it involuntarily made the ears of the assembly prick up.

It would be appropriate to replace "Gen" (艮) with "Shan" (山); the former signifies "stopping," while the latter signifies "mountain. One should substitute "stopping" for "mountain"—it requires changing only a single stroke.
I must honor the worthies of antiquity; I cannot help but act in this way.
To the heavenly youth Gan, who serves as a transformational practitioner for extending life:
in the household there is a skilled physician, yet illnesses have increased. There is no place to rest, and the speech is confused and erroneous. The water is like indigo, and the flowers are like—
Brocade. As before, the sound of raindrops drips upon the old eaves.

Once again carved is the speech of Dahui, which flowed forth from the breast of Miaoxi; it was personally inscribed by the Son of Heaven, Chonghua. Though the great trichiliocosm should all perish, this shall not.
It is destroyed. It is also permitted for him to publish it on separate wooden blocks.
Master Mingjian’s branch-stems are twenty-two golden nails. When transformations are infinite and inexhaustible, all people throughout the entire earth are nailed down.
In concentration: the Master knows it first; who else shall know it later?
The water-mill wheel has already turned for many moments. Its bitterness and astringency are clearly known only by oneself; rolling along, let the body go with the waves.
Rolling it along—onlookers gain eyes like eyebrows.
Not sparing the whole sweet melon, they approve it step by step; yet to bring it forth and speak of it is truly insatiable. Now, upon whom does this single slice fall?
In hand. To ensure sweetness, it must be sweet to the very core.

When one realizes their nature, the skull is drained of its dregs and the field of vision widens; a single, cold, perfectly clear and luminous pearl shines forth. Do not blame me for the dullness and confusion of recent years.
How true! The sound of the bell was outshone by the sound of the drum.
Standing in the snow at the Fangzhang Hall, the gate of Shaoshi was as cold as ice. Master Ke once paused and reflected upon this; at the end of the night, each knew the chill for himself.
It is cold. Do not wait until the snow reaches three feet deep.

On the single path across the Stone Bridge of Bodhi, the ground is as level as the palm of a hand; yet at every step one walks amidst the perils of wind and waves. Whether crossing horses or donkeys, do not hesitate.
Question: In ordinary circumstances, he seized the name of the Patriarch.
A single reed across the long river, a single reed and the waves part. The entire nation knows he will not come again; for a thousand ages, leaning upon the railing, one sighs in sorrow.
How regrettable! Who would have known that beneath one's feet it is as slippery as moss?

In the Hall of Dharma Adorned with Jewels, the old oyster vainly harbors the womb of the white moon; before the courtyard, the rain of flowers naturally piles up. I shall turn back the wind and thunder.
The tongue—needless to say, it does not come fluttering from all quarters to shake the earth.

Behold the willows by the mountain pavilion and the flowers along the city streets, blooming in profusion as one wanders; unaware that the sun and moon pass away like flowing water. Raising my eyes, I suddenly behold my native mountains.
Standing there, she covers her face with both hands in deep shame;
praise to the Buddha and Patriarchs for their manifestation in the form of leaving the mountains.
The Way has no cultivation or realization; why enter the mountains? The Dharma has no coming or going; where would you go upon leaving the mountains?
Golden palaces and mansions overgrown with weeds—before whom could one speak of this in heaven or among men?

For what reason did you enter the mountains for six years? And for what reason have you come forth from the mountains again? Your poisonous mind and poisonous conduct are difficult for others to perceive;
they see only your spring breeze-like smile as it unfolds.
Water-moon Avalokiteśvara:
the sky is cloudless, the ocean of nature is windless; the jade wheel dips its reflection, golden waves overturn the void.
Not only does Avalokiteśvara behold the world, but I too roam within it.
Contemplate the characteristics [of sound]:
spring birds sing by day and autumn insects chirp by night; all who have ears hear them—why should it be Avalokiteśvara alone? Know it thus.
Awakening in this manner, the face and eyes appear before one, surpassing all other studies.

Whether it be the warbling of swallows, the singing of orioles, the cawing of crows, or the chirping of magpies—their sounds differ from one another, yet hearing remains undistorted. Once the nature of hearing is stilled, [all is as it is].
The object of sound is also empty. A single point of compassionate mind is perfectly pervasive everywhere.
Opening one's eyes is entering samādhi;
the six faculties are as they are, their essence undivided. The ear can perceive form, and the eye can hear sound. Now that you are old and great, you should find peace.
[Fragment]. The eyes behold themselves and the ears hear themselves.
Zhao, the Prefectural Commissioner, requested a eulogy for the Avalokiteśvara with a rosary.
Floating on a lotus boat, the clouds of the heavens clear and the winds of the ocean of nature cease. Taking compassion as one’s heart, one rescues the multitudes.
Life is suffering. Taking compassion as one's eye, one observes the sorrows of sentient beings. What do sentient beings grieve over? They grieve over the neglect of internal cultivation.
What do sentient beings suffer from? They suffer from seeking after external things. Therefore, he manifests in the body of a high official (*kai-kwan*).

The laws of the official he proclaims do not go beyond being utterly loyal and filial, maintaining one’s reputation and integrity, preserving one’s salary and rank, and instructing one’s descendants so that they do not fall from their ancestral legacy. In this way, universally...
Nineteen classes of gates, thirty-two manifestations of the *Śūraṅgama*; with a joyful and smiling countenance, nodding in agreement.
As the days lengthen in the official hall and incense smoke drifts upward, I vow that my going and staying shall be one with your compassionate visage.
The fisherwoman holds her basket of fish in her left hand and lifts the hem of her robe with her right. Amidst the vast expanse of the dusty world, a single cry of life—
enough to open the eyes of those who could topple kingdoms and cities— and already ten thousand miles of white clouds have passed.

The spirit within the mirror of the Horse-herder’s Wife; her demeanor before the breeze, holding the Lotus Sutra in hand, changes the very entrails of men. The scaled fish swallows the bait and comes upon the hook;
the golden bones have already ascended into the void.
Mañjuśrī, clad in garments of grass, with his grass-like robes trailing and his hair hanging down, appears and disappears like a spirit; even the Buddha’s eye can hardly perceive him.
He could sit upon the tongue of Vimalakīrti, yet he could not emerge from the woman’s samādhi; he could carry out the commands of the Dharma King, yet he could not avoid Kāśyapa.
This doubt: the mountainous terrain of Wutai is steep and towering; he flings it back to him as a lion cub.
Mañjuśrī’s fearless lion’s roar speaks: in the empty space, he pushes; in the tight spot, he squeezes. That superior man has withdrawn his tongue; non-duality.
The gates are all in ruins. The Five-Tufted Youth, teacher of the seven Buddhas, instead proves himself a turtle becoming a white soft-shelled turtle.

Vimalakīrti rebukes the two vehicles and strikes down the ten stages, using forceful rhetoric to seize the correct principle. To the very end, the person who inquired after his illness—his words and...
Neither silence nor speech—this is the layman’s body of the Tathāgata Suvarṇaśālī. All the people of the entire earth cannot lift him up.
A hemp bag with a clumsy belly ten spans around; a shambling frame three feet tall. He breaks his staff and stirs the boundless seas of fragrant water, shattering...
A cloth bag holding ten billion Mount Sumerus—such is this person. *Siri siri*, seeking copper coins;
*sulu sulu*, neither in heaven nor on earth. The mountain colors of the Four Luminaries unfold like a painted scroll.
He stands holding a cloth bag; he takes the cloth bag and departs. When he descends to be born again in another day, he will utter a turning word elsewhere.
This Honored One of the Successive Seat plays with the real as if it were false; casting aside the inner palace, he comes to propagate the transformation.

Looking back at that time, the eyes within the skull have not yet ceased to flow. At the point of close reliance, the antiquities within the cloth bag cannot be laid down. If they can be laid down—[not yet].
One will inevitably encounter those who force one to paint [the Buddha].
Subhūti stands leaning on his staff, demonstrating true prajñā. As for the booklet in his hand, how could it be transcribed? Elder, if you do not...
Let go. Doubt kills the Venerable One of Later Birth.

He sat in constant meditation; he stood ever alert. A single expanse of empty stillness; ten thousand realms are void and silent. Before the crags, the rain of flowers has already fallen in profusion.
Fenggan and the Cold and Rake (Hanshan and Shide) only knew how to seize the tiger’s head, but they did not know how to grasp the tiger’s tail. If you expose others, others will also expose you.
Appearing and disappearing amidst the roar of tigers; rolling up and unfolding upon the tracks of oxen. Half is the play of children; half is the demeanor of adults.
Holding the cooking ladle, ashes cover his head; sweeping the floor, dust strikes his face. Contemplating deeply beneath the crag, it is clear: this whole affair is a failure to find one’s footing.
The Way brings no poverty; virtue has its neighbors. At the Five Peaks and the Twin Streams, who is host and who is guest? They lean against each other and sleep; the elephant king looks back.
They call out to one another and laugh; the lion yawns and groans. Alas! If you do not realize this meaning, [The following lines are omitted as they appear to be part of the original source text.]
The practitioner’s toil is bitter and arduous.
At the bottom of the twin ravines, before the five peaks, he grinds pine soot upon a block of stone. For every one or two characters produced, there are many failures;
yet when a few are achieved, they comprise the three hundred odes. Clearly, to whom does this meaning fall?

A gentle breeze blows through the rocky pines; the more one listens, the better it sounds, and the more one chants, the purer it becomes. This single phrase of the whole universe—its literary brilliance is exceedingly clear.
How could it ever be fully captured in writing?
The left hand holds a scroll; the right hand points. Revealed and exposed without concealment—who among many understands this meaning?
Turning the head, Mount Tai reveals its cold, verdant locks.
Clapping hands face to face, two mirrors reflecting one another; the twin ravines and five peaks break into laughter all at once on this cold ground.
To call this Samantabhadra is already to miss the mark.

Dharma sat with his face to the wall; to see this as a commodity for sale is to have missed the mark even while standing in the snow seeking him. One must know that such an offense is as vast as the heavens.
Coming, we toast with a cup of waves spanning a thousand acres; departing, we carry a single sandal through ten thousand layers of clouds. You say you transmit the Dharma—what Dharma do you transmit?
Thus I think of you, yet I also resent you.
Ten thousand waves and a thousand ripples, a single reed-raft crosses them. That solitary, fluttering figure is truly pitiable.
If Old Xiao understands the phrase of "cutting through the current," I shall let you go on your way at the head of the Yangtze River.
The orthodox eye of India from the six successive patriarchs, the mind-source of China: a single drop of ink-water forms two dragons;
to this day, it gives rise to a pure breeze throughout the land.
When all conditions cease, artifice is exhausted. There is constant, clear knowing—this is not "not," nor is it "is. Do not be deceived by foreign monks.
Within the ineffable, faith is extensively expounded; it is transparently clear, beyond past, future, and present. Thus, the wind-disorder [of conceptual thought] is cured.
It becomes even deeper.
The ancient Buddhas were without mind; who knows this? The Two Peaks nod their heads; the Stone Maiden frowns. Huangmei’s secret was wrongly entrusted to a mere child.
Able to go thus, able to return thus: the green pines are dense and lush, white hair is withered and frail.
When will news from south of the ridges arrive?

Though he does not recognize the characters, he is proficient in both the doctrine and its exposition. Like wind blowing over water, like the sun traveling through space, he has shattered the legacy of his ancestral craft.
This is that elder: the Venerable Master Baogong, the Great Being of the Eagle’s Nest.
His manifestations were boundless; he was born in the Song dynasty and lived out his old age during the Qi and Liang dynasties. With the knife and ruler upon his staff, he measured all things.
Hidden and manifest, all fully revealed. Sublime and majestic; brilliant and resplendent. To this day he sits, cutting off all at Dulong Peak.

In the Northern School, the Bodhi tree exists and the mirror is free from dust; the jade hare conceives within her womb as she enters the Purple Palace. The foremost among the seven hundred dragon-like monks.
The Abbot took the robe and offered it to the miller;
at Mount Dayu, the Head Monk could not lift it. One's original face remains as dusty as ever; the southern branches do not let the spring pass.
Rest! You are likewise a person caught in the vast, leaking net.

Heze, Heze—originally did not have the surname Gao. At the summit of the ridge, once cast in the net, it is ultimately difficult to escape. If you all do not deliberate upon this realization, [you will remain lost].
Explanation: To understand is to know that there is no cause for you to arrive at such a state.
Chan Master Xuefeng Zhenjue left the mountain ranges to transcend the mundane;

though he went up nine times and arrived three times, he was perfected by a single blow of the mallet. Yet even this was not yet "hot-tempered" enough—afterward, he recited the verse on crossing the water.

Hearing the meaning of the emptiness of form, my liver and intestines were churned; I could not sleep for sleeplessness. I received the essential point at the blow of the staff and clarified the fundamental principle beneath the phrase.
At the Turtle Mountain in the dead of night, it was like a crane casting off its cage; atop the high Elephant Bone Cliff, there lies the Turtle-Nose. Among the fifteen hundred people—
How many have been slandered? Three balls roll together at once. The Great Function is fully brought forth; even the spark of a flint cannot reach it, and the flash of lightning cannot pursue it.
The entire earth is gathered up like a grain of millet; practitioners of the past and present have looked at it but could not see beyond it—at Wàngzhōu and Wūshí.
Scorched by the sun and buffeted by the wind—ten thousand blessings upon you, Master Zeng! Your eyes are set above your eyebrows;
Puhua was such a "wind-monk" of extraordinary deportment. With a single shake of the wooden clapper, his voice reached the ears of all. He pointed directly at the place where my true self dwells.
He then set out. When biting raw vegetables, he would recoil at the slightest touch; whether facing light or facing darkness, he would turn away at the slightest pressure.
Today or yesterday, he would become intoxicated at the mere touch of support. Sometimes, in the hands of Daowu, he would reverse the spearhead;
sometimes, before the face of Linji, he would pour out a full vessel of foul water. With such skills, he was truly able to strip others of their defenses and establish the Huangbo lineage.
This is already the essence; how much more so when one acts recklessly and wildly, leaving a beginning but no end?

All such instances do not escape the prophecy of Dayang and the record of Panshan. If, at the very end, you do not seek a path of escape through the east, south, west, or north gates, you will certainly not avoid being laughed at by the "new bride," the "old woman’s Chan," and the "little servant boy," who will clap their hands and mock you.
Miao has attained the true likeness of his former master, yet their nostrils do not match. Returning to the Great Compassion Temple, the braying of a donkey is but a trifle.

While Xianzi’s Master dwells in a desolate village by an ancient shrine, others reside in jeweled palaces and lotus temples; while the Master dwells amidst piles of paper money, others wear jeweled necklaces.

Within the same assembly, while the Master gathers shrimp and clams, others strike at phoenixes and net dragons; while the Master’s fish are withered and parched, others enjoy jade-like delicacies in leisure and ease.
Thus, the Master and others differ in their concealment and manifestation, yet they are identical in their unfolding and rolling up.
As a younger brother of Huayan, he did not enter the protective society of Huayan; as a son of Dongshan, he did not inherit the gate-style of Dongshan.
Wishing to conceal one's traces, the traces become more prominent; wishing to obscure one's name, the name becomes more exalted.

Indeed, those who can be cautious at the beginning and guard against the end do not follow the cups and platters of others; no one knows what the Master knows, and the Master alone rejoices in his own joy—a joy that is inexhaustible.
If it were truly so, how could there be such a thing as "today"? To take a short ruler and measure empty space, or to grind a dull blade...
With ink, one attempts to fathom the vast void.

The ashes in the incense burner of the ancient temple are cold; the misty waters of the long river are chill. Though I have searched and sifted again and again, it is difficult to place upon the wine table.
The Yellow Ox Lake and the Lake Mountains are wondrous from every side; mist, clouds, wind, and moon are all new poems.
Where the悠然 (yōurán) spirit and meaning reach their limit, one even understands how to ride an ox as if it were a horse.
Shoulders hunched, the lake and mountains grow thin; eyes clear, the lake waters turn autumnal. Who is the companion for coming and going? The white egret and the yellow ox.

This is where Master Yushan’s donkey lost its footing at the mountain stream bridge; it is the moment of advancing further atop the hundred-foot pole. At that instant, head and heels are both changed at once.
It is finished. As before, it was simply Master Yujia riding a donkey across a bridge over a stream.
With one step, the bridge collapsed. Facing ten thousand peaks by the bridge, he clapped his hands and laughed without ceasing.
Dharma Flower says:
"Tearing one's robes to ascend the ninefold gates, I hurriedly took up my brush to write these thirteen lines. My mind dwells on neither end; as I depart, I again plot my journey south.
— The Sixteen Arhats.
The flying staff traverses the Five Indies as clouds drift on; the cup floats upon the South Sea where waves roll on and on. On the tip of a single hair, all is lightly gathered up;
were it not for karmic affinity, these would not meet head-to-head.
The Venerable One who crossed the river:
before the stream, the green waters swell as the first rain clears. A floating *lu* hat, its surface as level as a palm, at the heart of the waves.
Such is his skillful means from the start; let him go, hurrying forward on his journey ahead.
The morning sun pierces through the tattered robe;
standing before the eaves, one bears the warmth of the blazing sun. This ruined garment is mended with renewed effort;
the very lives of all people in the great earth are pinned fast upon the point of a single needle.
Waiting for the moon to finish reciting the sutras,
the old monk counts several black beans. When he finds his inspiration upon the rocks and at the roots of pines, he pities himself for this final phrase,
which only the bright moon at the edge of the sky may know.
The boatman monk’s wits and words accorded;
his phrases matched the head of the matter. Having been three inches beyond the hook, he had already swallowed it.
He cast away both the solitary boat and the short oars, until the waters of Zhujing flowed backward.
Master Liang’s mind was as vast as space;
before his lecture had ended, he called out once, turned his head, and revealed his countenance. Do not say that after he has departed there will be no news;
beyond the clouds, the western mountains’ emerald hues sweep across the void.
One who takes the Way as their principle wears a pair of straw sandals—without heels and without straps. They cannot be wrapped in a *kāṣāya* robe, nor can they be lifted by a staff.
Knowing only how to go barefoot to Tongcheng, they cannot avoid being laughed at by the people of Tongcheng.
The girl Lingzhao exhausted her family’s meager resources to sell a bamboo rake; who could have known such boundless wealth?
With hands folded before the wind, she uttered a single turning word—Dana might not necessarily have recognized her.
In the illustration of the Zen assembly, Huangbo holds the sandalwood staff;
who can shoulder the function of great capacity? The solitary wind of Duanji cannot be pursued; the youth of Jibei has yet to appear.
It is clear: Prince Fengguang already knew this beforehand.
Zhaozhou did not descend from his meditation seat to receive the two princes;

instead, he used a broken-legged meditation seat to receive the "broken firewood. Even so, he was still capable of sitting in a hunched posture to bow to a high guest. It is evident that their territories were vast and their influence reached the heavens.
Wealthy, yet difficult to contend with; though his family was impoverished to the bone, upon meeting the Emperor once, he established himself as a pillar of state, remaining firm and unmoving.
He stood upright with a majestic bearing, which was most fitting. Do not concern yourself with rising, sitting, walking, or pacing.
Outside. Separately, he sought to punish the Emperor of the Great Tang as his teacher.

Although Emperor Wenzong was fond of clams, a single point of compassion could not be split open. Amidst the boiling cauldrons, a smile filled his cheeks. This extraordinary matter, Your Majesty, I deeply [revere].
Xin has come from the presence of the Sovereign to preach the Dharma.
The treasure of the Central Plains was sought throughout the heavens and the earth;
this treasure of the Central Plains now conceals its form within the mountains. Had it not been presented to me, Old Xing, [it would have remained hidden].
Transformation. Often people treat this as something trivial.

When Li Ao visited the emaciated immortal at Mount Yaoshan beneath a thousand pine trees, he found a world of cold, distant mists and clouds—a realm entirely apart from the ordinary. The master bestowed upon him a mere "knife-edge" dose, yet it was fundamentally... [not for the faint of heart].
Consciousness returns to join hands at the edge of the waters and clouds.
When Pei Xiu offered a Buddha image and requested it be named, its true face was already fully revealed.
Bringing it forth to test the faculty of discernment, ten thousand Śākyamunis and myriad Maitreyas [are present].
Le! All is gathered within the light of a single body.
Han Yu requested further instruction:
"Leaving the realm, the road is far and long; The heart of return is set upon the Ninefold Heavens at eve. If one does not grasp it when the opportunity arises, one will not reach home."
Verse: For now, on the road ahead, quickly lay on the whip.
When Layman Pang saw Great Master Ma, the dragon’s head and horns were revealed as he churned the sea;
the tiger emerged from the forest, its claws and fangs bared. To this day, the wind and clouds stir throughout the six directions.
Inside. Vastly they come to ascend the field for selecting Buddhas.
Lingzhao, facing Danxia, reveals her wind and bearing;
this is the second mechanism. Even lightning and sparks are too slow. After Danxia departed, there was no one to receive [the transmission].
Rest. Furthermore, when seeing the iron gate firmly secured, speak words of non-arising to gather in the sentiments of mountain clouds and ocean moons.
Round and full, the nose is straight and the eyebrows arch; a whisk of tortoise hair and horns of a hare.
With his staff, he beats the void until it rings out with a sharp *pao pao* sound.
Lingzhao watches the rising and setting of the sun;
light and dark are paired, and one faculty seizes the other. Seeking advantage from her father’s hand, she truly proves that the old master is capable of being light-handed.
Faith. The sun has been surrendered at its zenith.
Pángdà leans on his hoe and passes away;
Lǎozǐ goes first but cannot reach the end. The young master’s final act is too extreme. Leaning against the sky, Mount Héng’s peaks are deep.
In this place, after the rain has passed, the cold light splashes before the eyes with clarity.

Praising the Fifth Patriarch of Dongshan, who rolls the embroidered ball and beats the earthen drum; half in the sound of Ba, half in the speech of Lu; heart and gall emptied, face and features revealed. It cannot be—
He could not be described nor fashioned; thus the world praised him, calling him the Patriarch of the Dongshan Lineage.
As for the life and conduct of Master Jiyuan Zhong, and his countenance:
clouds hung over the plains of Chu, and rain fell upon the mountains of Huai. Having examined his recorded sayings, [one sees this].
Beholding its functioning, it is like jade turning and pearls revolving, clouds arising and springs gushing forth; the Way of Jiyuan cannot be described in words.
That I now offer praise for it is like holding a measuring rod to measure empty space.
Master Beijian was refined in his antiquity and lofty in his character; his spirit was pure and his breath transcendent. Hearing a single word, he ascended the hall of the "Plain King" (Confucius);
seeing a subtle smile, he entered the chamber of the "Empty King" (the Buddha). Vast and expansive, he unified the myriad things through the One; silent and profound, he attained—
"Ten thousand things return to the One. Is this not indeed the eighty-third [verse]?
It was written by the old thief Beijian, a true son of Fozhao at Nanshan Jingci, who dwelt by the corner of the dragon-bed.

The thunder that breaks the hibernation of Master Chijue; the tortoise that points south; the jade axe that carves the circle; the golden pincers that scrape away the film. Alas! If not for this master, who else?
The Elder Guangfu Cong painted a portrait of Wuzhun’s crown-protrusion and requested a eulogy for this Compassionate Honored One.
[Wuzhun] once composed a self-eulogy: "It cannot be boiled to maturity; it cannot be burned to ruin. It possesses a stubborn softness and lacks calculation.
Weighing Mount Sumeru, it registers four *liang*; measuring empty space, it spans one and a half *zhang*. Furthermore, there is a white hair in an improper place, which he has entrusted to none."
Hearing this, I shall judge it according to principle.
Self-Praise for Elder Ché of Donglin; Requested to Write a Eulogy.

With the appearance of one who withered first at a cold riverbank, and the integrity of one whose character remains undecayed in ancient crags, snow fills his head—nothing but a taste of frigid austerity;
clouds rest upon his shoulders—tenfold parched and withered. Whether going or staying as circumstances permit, there is abundance wherever he is; whatever comes to hand, he grasps it with confidence.
The timing is exactly right. Although it is said that principle transcends thought, how can one help but harbor it within the affairs of the world?
A long sword leaning against the heavens must be sharpened when used; it is now entrusted to the Elder Mingyan Che.
At the request of Elder Huichang of Tiger Hill, I offer this eulogy:
Ten thousand miles of clear sky, a single clap of thunder—no one throughout the great earth can cover their ears fast enough.
A vast, pure wind arises across the eight directions.
At Xiangfu, Elder Xi requests a eulogy for Sanyan:
When the sun warms the ground for walking meditation, And the breeze clears the air at the time of seated repose at Shuangjing— In the past you were not young, and now you are not old;
How can one depict you so that others may know?
At the request of Elder Sun Fu, a disciple of Master Yuantong, I offer this eulogy:
Vast and empty space is my essence; the myriad phenomena in their profusion are my function. Green mountains and white clouds—
The mountain colors and the sounds of the stream are my companions; the discourse of the mountains and streams is my speech.
One who makes such a claim is beyond the power of even a master painter to conjure. As for that which even a master painter cannot conjure, I do not know who I am.
Therefore, I have given myself this forced name: the Old Frost-Bitten Farmer of Shikishima.
At the request of the Elder Zishou Qin, I offer this eulogy for the appearance of Hanpu Xianling and his integrity that withers last among the ancient crags. Snow fills his head—purely austere;
clouds embrace his shoulders—tenfold withered. He dwells according to conditions, having abundance wherever he touches; he responds according to the occasion.
There is nothing that cannot be accommodated. The family laws are stern and rigorous; the hammer and tongs are coarse and violent—who can withstand them?
Take Elder Zhun, for instance, or Elder Jing of Western India, who requested a eulogy on "form and sight, sound and seeking.
Both are not it. Apart from sound and form, one turns up empty-handed. Amidst the flash of a stone flint, [the truth] is revealed.
In a flash of lightning, one must see Shixi; do not nod off to sleep!
Layman Yang requests a eulogy for the moon in the water and the form in the mirror: a head of spring snow and half a shoulder of autumn clouds—behold them, yet behold them not.
It is called "right contemplation. To hear while there is no hearing is called "true hearing. When a painter depicts you, you are I;
when a layman recognizes me, I am not you. "This" and "not this," divided yet undivided—praising or slandering them is merely idle chatter.
The junior disciple Zhenggong has transcribed the "Seclusion Chamber" (Yanshi) of Songyuan and the "Diagram of Master Shan’s Journey," requesting a eulogy.
The father goes before; the son follows behind. This unworthy grandson is both foolish and deluded. As for the gates of samādhi, each knows them for themselves.
Entering the deep village, the weeds grow tall and lush; before the wind, I recall old Yangqi.
A single cloud clears away; ten thousand phenomena appear in the ancient pool. Whence does it come so lightly? Whither does it go so serenely?
To recognize it is not to recognize it; to know it is to have no knowing. Who is it that breaks through the iron walls and silver mountains?
A minor Buddhist service:
Zen Master Shitoku enters the Patriarchs’ Hall.
Having fully possessed the splendor of the mountains north and south, he turns his body around; the old garden is reclaimed as idle fields.
The ground is established separately with a style of discipline that is utterly fresh and new.

We respectfully venerate Master Shitai, the thirty-fourth patriarch of Beishan, who sits upon the Vulture Peak and manifests his body at Baoshou. At this very moment, what is it to depart? What is it to remain?
If one departs, the mountain stream lingers on and the mountain clouds hold fast. If one remains, Nantong beckons and the local spirit stands guard.
[The Master] nods his head. After all, how is it? "A single hall, wind and cold; the meaning of ten thousand ages is clear.
Master Kuzhang enters the Patriarchs’ Hall and calls to the assembly, saying:
"Do you know where Master Kuzhang has landed? His entire life was one of straightforwardness and distinctiveness. A precipice..."
A rugged cliff; raw iron for a mask, stubborn rock for a breast. Unchanging through spring, difficult to bury even where the earth opens.

Having chosen his dwelling in the heart of the Yangtze River, his evil reputation has already been inscribed upon the memorial tablet. Pointing to the tablet, he said: "The nameplate is here; where is the withered stump?
If you say it is everywhere, it is still as far apart as heaven and earth. If you say it is not there, it is very much like..."
Never having held a formal vegetarian feast—how, ultimately, is this so? For a thousand ages, the ancestral hall’s wind remains chillingly stern; do not say there is no position to be arranged.
The Master Wuzu enters his stupa.
The mountains of Zhedong; the waters of Zhewest. Breaking off the head of my staff, no wind stirs the waves. Several times I have borne the burden of falling into the pure depths;
with a single laugh, we dwell together. With whom today shall I discuss this mind? The myriad phenomena and all living beings alike lean their ears toward it.
In the hall of Mount Jing, the Great Monk Chan Master Fojian has established the *Wannian Zhengxu* (The True Succession of Myriad Years) as the definitive transmission for an era. Ten...

For eight years he sat atop the summit of Five Peaks; there, amidst hundreds of thousands of samādhis, he roamed the stage of illusory drama. Secret signs were communicated in silence, and the true mechanism was entrusted in secrecy.
Grasping and releasing both simultaneously, half-closing and half-opening, only then was he fit for this single principle shared by one heart.
Yet it was not anticipated that the brothers would cross paths in ten directions: where the body is hidden, no trace remains; in the clear pool and azure sea lies the mud ox.
Do not hide yourself where there are no traces. A stone tiger crouches on the western ridge and the eastern mountain. In the midst of the blazing summer heat, snow and ice fill the streets;
under the bright, clear sky, a sudden thunderclap shakes the earth. At such a time, the gate of the pagoda opens once and, having been entered, closes again.
How do you express this in a single phrase? At that moment, white clouds completely cover all, and there is no more moonlight in the four directions.
Shanliu: Master Chijue entered the Patriarchs’ Hall and called to the assembly, saying, “The former master of this mountain, Master Chijue, has returned. Do you see him? Liang.
Jiuyun said: In years past, I left Mount Taibai for Mount Ling; a single white cloud drifted back and forth through the void. Last year, I took my leave of Mount Mao to ascend Mount Fahua;
where could such lofty traces not be my home? This morning, we meet at the Double Path (Shuangjing);
the ancient inscriptions have faded as the sun stands at its zenith. At this moment, who is host and who is guest? We gaze into one another’s eyes and abide thus.
Abiding thus, what need is there for a phoenix to wait for the wutong tree?
When he encountered Chan Master Yuan, the Head Seat, entering the stupa, his backbone was as hard as iron;
for over seventy years it remained unbent, until it fell into the furnace of Mount Zhong.
In the midst [of this], the furnace has forged the heavens of the Blazing Radiance into flakes of snow.
I wish to gather and wrap them with a seamless cloth, yet I fear I cannot wrap them all; I wish to scatter and conceal them within the Sutureless Stūpa, yet I fear I cannot conceal them completely.
Ultimately, how is it? Encountering the Hermitage, encountering the Hermitage—you should resolve this for yourself.
When Master Guishan of Zhaojue dug up the earth and stirred up the Sichuan road with sharp blades, the sun and moon were darkened;
yet the Hermitage remained unharmed. When the fires of the kalpa incinerated the heavens of Sichuan, [the Hermitage] was empty.

The world was reduced to ashes and embers, yet the earthen hermitage did not burn. For thirty years, there was one departure and one remaining, yet there was no distinction between departing and staying.
Eight thousand li separated "there" and "here," yet there was no differentiation between self and other. At such a time as this, how is it?
It divides and shatters the clouds upon the western peaks of the North Mountain; at night, it coldly illuminates Mount Emei.
Where wisdom turns back and the seat is locked within the niche, it is where wisdom does not reach.
It is entirely hidden and entirely revealed; it turns back and interpenetrates sideways, yet remains identical to defilement. One must leap across this with all one’s might.
He emerged; his entire body remained within. The single room was vast and empty, idle all day long. Yet one must further lock off the path of frantic rushing.
Master Shufu, in the midst of the clamor where the funeral pyre is lit, you plant your feet in stillness. How magnificent, Master Shufu! Raising the torch, he said: "Pass through this!"
Attaching. This attachment and that attachment—opening the eyes, one attaches; closing the eyes, one attaches.

Elder Qing’s extinguishing of the fire was utterly pure, reaching a state of boundless transcendence. Yet such a source of illness continued to flow without ceasing; last night, it was thoroughly exhausted.
It is all overturned. Before every door is a torch.
Upasaka Xin of Jizhou has the implements for lighting the fire;
he possesses decisive faith. In what does he believe? It accords with the price of rice in Luling. Directly beneath, there are no two.
If it is so with the stage of faith, how is it with the human stage? [The Master] throws down a torch and says:
"It must not be called fire. Master Jian locks the shrine;
his adamantine body is utterly without reliance. Within every single atom, he abides in this manner. Master Jian, take hold of it once!
The secure barrier is firmly locked. Take it for granted that the full moon shall appear before the door.
As for Upādhya Āyuṣmān Rong, let the withered remain withered and let the flourishing remain flourishing; he does not trespass upon either extreme. A single blade naturally gives rise to the wind.
"Do not walk where you have walked before. Master Rong, where then do you walk? When you mount a horse, you see the road;
when Master Jue mounts the fire, he does not worry about its arising. He only fears that his awakening is late. Awakening, too, is an illness. What medicine can cure it? Let go of everything."
Contemplate this: when refined gold enters the fire, it naturally radiates its own brilliance.
Disciple Zong, extinguish the fire.
This one school of ours is difficult to obtain; yet even if obtained, it is easy to lose, while it is difficult to transmit—difficult beyond measure. To the west of the city...
"The White Snow and Yangchun Melodies—today I shall clearly perform them for you once. He threw a torch and said, "Quickly, look with your eyes!

When Master Li was about to enter the fire, [the Master] asked, "The principle is thus; what of the phenomenon? [Master Li] gave a shout on the spot and, shaking his sleeves, departed. If one investigates to this extent...
There is no place for involvement; it is precisely right to cast one’s entire body into the fire pit.
When Master Hai lowered the heart of fire, the green moss grew directly beneath him; at the gate of the sea, red flames arose. For forty-four or forty-five years, he practiced only until this point.
Even this is not yet it. As for the Brahmin Jvalamukha’s mass of fire and mountain of knives—look at you, Head Monk Hai;
meeting the occasion, you perform your play by casting fire directly into the water.
He drew a line with his finger and said: "This single path—tread upon it and you have it. How many times have you stirred the water seeking the waves?
How many times have you stirred the waves seeking the water? At the third watch of the night, while washing your face, you have pointlessly felt for your mother’s nose."
Having felt it, what then? One leaps headlong into a pit of fire. It requires you to have no wind when the waves arise;
it is the ailment that the attendant Zhiyuan cannot manage with the gathering of fires, the medicine that cannot be swallowed by mere words. Attendant Zhiyuan, know this only for yourself.
The world’s finest physicians do not know where to apply their skill; Attendant Yuan, however, knows his own ground.
Having cast everything aside, he carries a torch into the cowshed—step by step, higher and higher.
When the Seated Elder of the Seal goes out with fire, the seal remains;
when he raises his eyebrows and his eyes stare fixedly, the seal is broken. Abiding, the seal is shattered; up, down, the four cardinal directions, and the four intermediate points all belong to me.
Going and staying are the same as when the seal is broken: the clear pool does not permit the azure dragon to lie. At this very moment—
"How is it? When the weather is cold, one should simply turn toward the fire.

As for selecting the person to light the funeral pyre—the master of the stupa—who is truly discerning? His eyes are piercing and his nose is straight; though they walk together, they do not know one another. In vain do you say..."
This year I am seventy-seven. (He strikes a circle with his staff and says: Do you see it? To choose the root of perfect penetration—this is the foremost.
*The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Shixi Fohai*, Volume Lower (End).
Preface to the Newly Added *Taming Mara* Illustrations (with Introduction):

At the beginning of the Buddha’s appearance in the world, the forces of Māra and externalists were rampant. There was a demoness with a thousand sons, whose various species were exceedingly numerous; they devoured human beings.
Children are a source of affliction both in heaven and among humans. Thereupon, the Buddha took his most beloved son and covered him with a lapis lazuli bowl.
When the mother lost her child, she wept and searched for him everywhere. The Buddha called her to come and pointed out her son, returning him to her.
The demoness mother mobilized all her subordinate troops and exerted every supernatural power, yet she could not move the bowl. The Buddha asked, "What of your beloved son?"
"Is this the same as loving one's own child, or is it different? The ghost mother repented, prostrated herself, and made a vow:
"From this day forward, I shall regard the children of others as my own children. If there are those who pray for children, I shall fulfill their supplications.
As soon as she had formed this resolve, the bowl opened by itself, and she departed carrying her child in her arms.
The Dharma is ten feet high; Māra is ten feet high. It is simply that the heterodox and the orthodox follow divergent paths. Tradition says:

when even a slight thought arises, one is immediately encompassed by the realms of the *ālayavijñāna* (the hidden realm). One dwells amidst the palaces of Māra and the dens of ghosts, wandering through the murky long night, dreaming with eyes closed, reaching everywhere.
The Buddha, pitying them, employs the radiance of great wisdom—like the sun suspended in the sky—to shatter those [darknesses].
From the depths of darkness, he caused all to open their eyes and see the light, abandoning error to return to the correct path.
Through the samādhi of the painter’s brush-tip, he conjured this "Diagram of the Subduing of Māra," which contains profound intent.

Those who contemplate this diagram—if they can suddenly perceive the thoughts of good and evil, or the deviant and the correct, before they have even taken form—then who is the Buddha and who is Māra? If this is not yet the case, one should nevertheless [reflect upon it].
A Self-Exhortation. Written on the tenth day after the Double Ninth Festival in the year of Yisi (1245) during the Chunyou era, by the old monk Shixi Xin Yue, abbot of Mount Huqiu, at Cishuang.
After Inscribing the Calligraphy of Layman Duanzhai:
High-minded men and realized scholars of the past, such as Wang Xizhi and Tao Yuanming, have never failed to enter our protective community.
The great masters of our own dynasty, such as Dongpo and Huanggu, were likewise those who entered and exited with playful ease. Written by Shulou Duan.

The layman Cai was bold, unrestrained, and magnificent; his character and temperament were refined and unburdened. In his later years, he lived in seclusion at the foot of Feilai Peak, where monks from all quarters trod upon his threshold.
Xinyue, owing to their long-standing ties as fellow villagers, returned to Lengquan, where they remained deeply affectionate toward one another from beginning to end.
Whatever the layman uttered—whether in jest, laughter, anger, or reproach—all became literary compositions. This alone is the inscription he composed for Haishang.
Bound by the ties of this world, it was only after his passing that I was finally able to behold him clearly.
Although I no longer see the Layman Sīha, the air of his transcendence still lingers here in a faint semblance. Written on the立夏 (Lìxì) day of the Gēngxū year of the Chúnyu era by Shíxī Xīnyuè.
The Old Man of Cangzhou, while observing at the Fish Bay Hermitage by the Tiaoxi River,
on the day Ding-si of the second month in the year Xinhai of the Chunyou era, composed the *Kai Guangming zang shu* (Commentary on the Opening of the Treasury of Light).

In the *Dàguāngmíngzàng* (The Great Luminous Treasury), Tán Shǎoyún of Júzhōu took up the historian’s brush to investigate and compile the karmic conditions and dialogues of the Buddhas and patriarchs, arranging them into this written record so that students may examine their ultimate purport. This will provide no small benefit to the Gate of the Patriarchs.
Thereafter, people transcribed it, vying with one another to treasure it; consequently, the authentic and the spurious became intermingled.
The Zen practitioner Siming of Sijia examined and corrected the original edition for publication. It requires fellow practitioners and worthy gentlemen to assist in its propagation and elucidation.
He spoke again in verse: [Verse omitted as per instructions]
The true life-vein was personally transmitted by the Buddhas and Patriarchs; from the brush of Juzu, its source flows forth. Its radiant brilliance extends for a hundred thousand fathoms;
it values nothing more than the transmission of a single seal to one who understands.
Written on the day of the *pravāraṇā* ceremony in the year of Bǎoyòu Yìmǎo (1255) by Shìxī Xīnyuè of Jìngshān.

This was shown to the Chan practitioner Wúxiàng Jìngzhào, who traveled across the sea to visit him. Before long, his demeanor and gestures were revealed to be extraordinary; thus, [the following] was composed.
I have read the verse you showed me; it is most admirable. If one emulates the footsteps of the former sages, there is no need to worry about not walking hand-in-hand with them.
A monk asked Zhaozhou, "What is it like when one brings nothing at all? Zhaozhou said, "Put it down.
The monk said, "When I bring nothing at all, what is there to put down? Zhaozhou said, "If you cannot put it down, then carry it away. The monk attained great enlightenment.
At these words, tell me: where exactly is this monk’s place of awakening? Try to discern it for yourself; you must not concern yourself with whether you understand or not.
You should take awakening as your standard. As it is said, "Do not worry about not being able to walk hand-in-hand with the sages of old.
You should stand firm and await the moment of realization. Strive accordingly. Written at Mount Jing on the first month of winter in the year of Yi-mao.
The Old Bhikṣu Śin-yueh offers these mountain verses as a parting gift to the Chan practitioner Chun of the Nine Rivers,
who returns to Donglin to receive instruction under Master Lingyin. By Shixi, Śin-yueh.
In recent years, the Buddha-dharma has been muddled by errors; ten thousand or a hundred thousand cases do not exceed this. I send word to Donglin:
raise your hand slightly and see what his eyes and mind are like.
Written on the Mid-Autumn Festival of the Chunyi year at Mount One Peak (Yīfēng) of Lingjiu.
The old monk Shíxī of Línghyìn sends this verse to the Chan practitioner Chún; its phrasing transcends the expectations of men, and the luster of its ink illuminates both past and present.
